entries.0c1668946fb73cdf5c29ea721b91a83751d31779: <div sID="gen25644" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Luke.9" sID="Luke.9"/> <div eID="gen25644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25645" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25646" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The commission Christ gave to his twelve apostles to go out for some time to preach the gospel, and confirm it by miracles, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.1-Luke.9.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. Herod's terror at the growing greatness of our Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.7-Luke.9.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. III. The apostles' return to Christ, his retirement with them into a place of solitude, the great resort of people to them notwithstanding, and his feeding five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.10-Luke.9.17">ver. 10-17</reference>. IV. His discourse with his disciples concerning himself and his own sufferings for them, and their for him, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.18-Luke.9.27">ver. 18-27</reference>. V. Christ's transfiguration, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.28-Luke.9.36">ver. 28-36</reference>. VI. The cure of a lunatic child, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.37-Luke.9.42">ver. 37-42</reference>. VII. The repeated notice Christ gave his disciples of his approaching sufferings, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.43-Luke.9.45">ver. 43-45</reference>. VIII. His check to the ambition of his disciples (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.46-Luke.9.48">ver. 46-48</reference>), and to their monopolizing the power over devils to themselves, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.49-Luke.9.50">ver. 49, 50</reference>. IX. The rebuke he gave them for an over-due resentment of an affront given him by a village of the Samaritans, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.51-Luke.9.56">ver. 51-56</reference>. X. The answers he gave to several that were inclined to follow him, but not considerately, or not zealously and heartily, so inclined, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.57-Luke.9.62">ver. 57-62</reference>.
entries.bfe9c1f7d9baafc2b80cd279229041239572dd4d: <div eID="gen25646" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25645" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Mission of the Twelve Apostles.</title> <div sID="gen25647" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then he called his twelve disciples together, and gave them power and authority over all devils, and to cure diseases. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he sent them to preach the kingdom of God, and to heal the sick. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he said unto them, Take nothing for <hi type="italic">your</hi> journey, neither staves, nor scrip, neither bread, neither money; neither have two coats apiece. <hi type="super">4</hi> And whatsoever house ye enter into, there abide, and thence depart. 5 And whosoever will not receive you, when ye go out of that city, shake off the very dust from your feet for a testimony against them. <hi type="super">6</hi> And they departed, and went through the towns, preaching the gospel, and healing every where. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him: and he was perplexed, because that it was said of some, that John was risen from the dead; <hi type="super">8</hi> And of some, that Elias had appeared; and of others, that one of the old prophets was risen again. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Herod said, John have I beheaded: but who is this, of whom I hear such things? And he desired to see him. <div eID="gen25647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25648" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The method Christ took to spread his gospel, to diffuse and enforce the light of it. He had <hi type="italic">himself</hi> travelled about, preaching and healing; but he could be only in one place at a time, and therefore now he <hi type="italic">sent</hi> his twelve disciples abroad, who by this time were pretty well instructed in the nature of the present dispensation, and able to instruct others and <hi type="italic">deliver to them</hi> what they had <hi type="italic">received from the Lord.</hi> Let them disperse themselves, some one way and some another, to <hi type="italic">preach the kingdom of God,</hi> as it was now about to be set up by the Messiah, to make people acquainted with the spiritual nature and tendency of it, and to persuade them to come into the interests and measures of it. For the confirming of their doctrine, because it was new and surprising, and very different from what they had been taught by the scribes and Pharisees, and because so much depended upon men's receiving, or not receiving it, he empowered them to work miracles (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.1-Luke.9.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): He <hi type="italic">gave them authority over all devils,</hi> to dispossess them, and cast them out, though ever so numerous, so subtle, so fierce, so obstinate. Christ designed a total rout and ruin to the kingdom of darkness, and therefore gave them power over <hi type="italic">all</hi> devils. He authorized and appointed them likewise to <hi type="italic">cure disease,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">heal the sick,</hi> which would make them welcome wherever they came, and not only convince people's judgments, but gain their affections. This was their commission. Now observe, <div eID="gen25648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25649" type="x-p"/> 1. What Christ directed them to do, in prosecution of this commission at this time, when they were not to <hi type="italic">go far</hi> or be <hi type="italic">out long.</hi> (1.) They must not be solicitous to recommend themselves to people's esteem by their outward appearance. Now that they begin to set up for themselves, they must have no dress, nor study to make any other figure than what they made while they followed him: they must <hi type="italic">go as they were,</hi> and not change their clothes, or so much as put on a pair of new shoes. (2.) They must depend upon Providence, and the kindness of their friends, to furnish them with what was convenient for them. They must not take with them <hi type="italic">either bread or money,</hi> and yet believe they should not want. Christ would not have his disciples <hi type="italic">shy</hi> of receiving the kindnesses of their friends, but rather to <hi type="italic">expect</hi> them. Yet St. Paul saw cause not to go by this rule, when he <hi type="italic">laboured with his hands</hi> rather than be burdensome. (3.) They must not change their lodgings, as suspecting that those who entertained them were <hi type="italic">weary</hi> of them; they have no reason to be so, for the ark is a guest that always pays well for its entertainment: "<hi type="italic">Whatsoever house ye enter into there abide</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.4">v. 4</reference>), that people may know where to find you, that your friends may know you are not backward to <hi type="italic">serve</hi> them, and your enemies may know you are not ashamed nor afraid to <hi type="italic">face</hi> them; <hi type="italic">there abide</hi> till you <hi type="italic">depart</hi> out of that city; stay with those you are used to." (4.) They must put on authority, and speak <hi type="italic">warning</hi> to those who <hi type="italic">refused</hi> them as well as comfort to those that <hi type="italic">received</hi> them, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.5">v. 5</reference>. "If there be any place that will not entertain you, if the magistrates deny you admission and threaten to treat you as vagrants, leave them, do not force yourselves upon them, nor run yourselves into danger among them, but at the same time bind them over to the judgment of God for it; <hi type="italic">shake off the dust of your feet</hi> for a <hi type="italic">testimony against them.</hi>" This will, as it were, be produced in evidence against them, that the messengers of the gospel had been among them, to make them a fair offer of grace and peace, for this dust they left behind there; so that when they perish at last in their infidelity this will lay and leave their blood upon their own heads. <hi type="italic">Shake off the dust of your feet,</hi> as much as to say you abandon their city, and will have no more to do with them. <div eID="gen25649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25650" type="x-p"/> 2. What they did, in prosecution of this commission (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">They departed</hi> from their Master's presence; yet, having still his spiritual presence with them, his <hi type="italic">eye</hi> and his <hi type="italic">arm</hi> going along with them, and, thus borne up in their work, they <hi type="italic">went through the towns,</hi> some or other of them, all the towns within the circuit appointed them, <hi type="italic">preaching the gospel, and healing every where.</hi> Their work was the same with their Master's, doing good both to souls and bodies. <div eID="gen25650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25651" type="x-p"/> II. We have here Herod's perplexity and vexation at this. The communicating of Christ's power to those who were sent forth in his name, and acted by authority from him, was an <hi type="italic">amazing</hi> and <hi type="italic">convincing</hi> proof of his being the Messiah, above any thing else; that he could not only work miracles <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> but empower others to work miracles too, this spread his fame more than any thing, and made the rays of this <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness</hi> the stronger by the <hi type="italic">reflection</hi> of them even from <hi type="italic">the earth,</hi> from such mean illiterate men as the apostles were, who had nothing else to recommend them, or to raise any expectations from them, but that <hi type="italic">they had been with Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Acts iv. 13</reference>. When the country sees such as these <hi type="italic">healing the sick</hi> in the name of Jesus it gives it an alarm. Now observe, <div eID="gen25651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25652" type="x-p"/> 1. The <hi type="italic">various speculations</hi> it <hi type="italic">raised</hi> among the <hi type="italic">people,</hi> who, though they thought not <hi type="italic">rightly,</hi> yet could not but think <hi type="italic">honourably,</hi> of our Lord Jesus, and that he was an extraordinary person, one come from the other world; that either John Baptist, who was lately persecuted and slain for the cause of God, or <hi type="italic">one of the old prophets,</hi> that had been persecuted and slain long since in that cause, was <hi type="italic">risen again,</hi> to be recompensed for his sufferings by this honour put upon him; or that Elias, who was taken alive to heaven in a fiery chariot, <hi type="italic">had appeared</hi> as an express from heaven, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.7-Luke.9.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen25652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25653" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">great perplexity</hi> it <hi type="italic">created</hi> in the mind of Herod: <hi type="italic">When he had heard of all that was done</hi> by Christ, his guilty conscience flew in his face, and he was ready to conclude with them that <hi type="italic">John was risen from the dead.</hi> He thought he had got clear of John, and should never be troubled with him any more, but, it seems, he is mistaken; either John is come to life again or here is another in his spirit and power, for God will never <hi type="italic">leave himself without witness.</hi> "What shall I do now?" saith Herod. "John <hi type="italic">have I beheaded, but who is this?</hi> Is he carrying on John's work, or is he come to avenge John's death? John baptized, but he does not; <hi type="italic">John did no miracle,</hi> but he does, and therefore appears more formidable than John." Note, Those who oppose God will find themselves more and more <hi type="italic">embarrassed.</hi> However, he <hi type="italic">desired to see him,</hi> whether he resembled John or no; but he might soon have been put out of this pain if he would but have informed himself of that which thousands knew, that Jesus preached, and wrought miracles, a great while before John was beheaded, and therefore could not be John raised from the dead. He <hi type="italic">desired to see him;</hi> and why did he not go and see him? Probably, because he thought it <hi type="italic">below him</hi> either to go to him or to send for him; he had enough of John Baptist, and cared not for having to do with any more such reprovers of sin. He desired to see him, but we do not find that ever he did, till he saw him at his bar, and then <hi type="italic">he and his men of war set him at nought,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.23.11">Luke xxiii. 11</reference>. Had he prosecuted his convictions now, and gone to see him, who knows but a happy change might have ben wrought in him? But, delaying it now, his heart was hardened, and when he did see him he was as much prejudiced against him as any other.
entries.4d9830ec8e49fb03bea763510c7541f0ae5d9fd3: <div eID="gen25653" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Multitude Miraculously Fed.</title> <div sID="gen25654" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And the apostles, when they were returned, told him all that they had done. And he took them, and went aside privately into a desert place belonging to the city called Bethsaida. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the people, when they knew <hi type="italic">it,</hi> followed him: and he received them, and spake unto them of the kingdom of God, and healed them that had need of healing. <hi type="super">12</hi> And when the day began to wear away, then came the twelve, and said unto him, Send the multitude away, that they may go into the towns and country round about, and lodge, and get victuals: for we are here in a desert place. <hi type="super">13</hi> But he said unto them, Give ye them to eat. And they said, We have no more but five loaves and two fishes; except we should go and buy meat for all this people. 14 For they were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, Make them sit down by fifties in a company. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they did so, and made them all sit down. <hi type="super">16</hi> Then he took the five loaves and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed them, and brake, and gave to the disciples to set before the multitude. <hi type="super">17</hi> And they did eat, and were all filled: and there was taken up of fragments that remained to them twelve baskets. <div eID="gen25654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25655" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The account which the twelve gave their Master of the success of their ministry. They were not long out; but, <hi type="italic">when they returned, they told him all that they had done,</hi> as became servants who were sent on an errand. They told him <hi type="italic">what they had done,</hi> that, if they had done any thing amiss, they might mend it next time. <div eID="gen25655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25656" type="x-p"/> II. Their <hi type="italic">retirement,</hi> for a little <hi type="italic">breathing:</hi> He <hi type="italic">took them, and went aside privately into a desert place,</hi> that they might have some relaxation from business and not be always upon the stretch. Note, He that hath appointed our man-servant and maid-servant to rest would have his servants to rest too. Those in the most public stations, and that are most publicly useful, must sometimes go aside privately, both for the repose of their bodies, to recruit them, and for the furnishing of their minds by meditation for further public work. <div eID="gen25656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25657" type="x-p"/> III. The <hi type="italic">resort</hi> of the people to him, and the kind <hi type="italic">reception</hi> he gave them. They <hi type="italic">followed</hi> him, though it was into a <hi type="italic">desert place;</hi> for that is no desert where Christ is. And, though they hereby disturbed the repose he designed here for himself and his disciples, yet he <hi type="italic">welcomed</hi> them, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, Pious zeal may excuse a little rudeness; it did with Christ, and should with us. Though they came unseasonably, yet Christ gave them what they came for. 1. He <hi type="italic">spoke unto them of the kingdom of God,</hi> the laws of that kingdom with which they must be bound, and the privileges of that kingdom with which they might be blessed. 2. He <hi type="italic">healed them that had need of healing,</hi> and, in a sense of their need, made their application to him. Though the disease was ever so inveterate, and incurable by the physicians, though the patients were ever so poor and mean, yet Christ <hi type="italic">healed them.</hi> There is healing in Christ for all that <hi type="italic">need</hi> it, whether for soul or body. Christ hath still a power over bodily diseases, and heals his people that <hi type="italic">need healing.</hi> Sometimes he sees that we need the <hi type="italic">sickness</hi> for the good of our souls, more than the <hi type="italic">healing</hi> for the ease of our bodies, and then we must be willing <hi type="italic">for a season,</hi> because <hi type="italic">there is need,</hi> to be in <hi type="italic">heaviness;</hi> but, when he sees that we <hi type="italic">need healing,</hi> we shall have it. Death is his servant, to heal the saints of <hi type="italic">all diseases.</hi> He heals spiritual maladies by his graces, by his comforts, and has for each what the case calls for; relief for every exigence. <div eID="gen25657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25658" type="x-p"/> IV. The plentiful provision Christ made for the multitude that attended him. With <hi type="italic">five loaves</hi> of bread, and <hi type="italic">two fishes,</hi> he fed <hi type="italic">five thousand men.</hi> This narrative we had twice before, and shall meet with it again; it is the only miracle of our Saviour's that is recorded by all the four evangelists. Let us only observe out of it, 1. Those who diligently attend upon Christ in the way of duty, and therein deny or expose themselves, or are made to forget themselves and their outward conveniences by their zeal for God's house, are taken under his particular care, and may depend upon <hi type="italic">Jehovah-jireh—The Lord will provide.</hi> He will not see those that fear him, and serve him faithfully, want any good thing. 2. Our Lord Jesus was of a free and generous spirit. His disciples said, <hi type="italic">Send them away, that they may get victuals;</hi> but Christ said, "No, <hi type="italic">give ye them to eat;</hi> let what we have go as far as it will reach, and they are welcome to it." Thus he has taught both ministers and Christians to <hi type="italic">use hospitality without grudging,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.9">1 Pet. iv. 9</reference>. Those that have but a little, let them do what they can with that little, and that is the way to make it more. <hi type="italic">There is that scatters, and yet increases.</hi> 3. Jesus Christ has not only physic, but food, for all those that by faith apply themselves to him; he not only <hi type="italic">heals them that need healing,</hi> cures the diseases of the soul, but feeds them too that need feeding, supports the spiritual life, relieves the necessities of it, and satisfies the desires of it. Christ has provided not only to save the soul from perishing by its diseases, but to nourish the soul unto life eternal, and strengthen it for all spiritual exercises. 4. All the gifts of Christ are to be received by the church in a regular orderly manner; <hi type="italic">Make them sit down by fifties in a company,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.14">v. 14</reference>. Notice is here taken of the number of each company which Christ appointed for the better distribution of the meat and the easier computation of the number of the guests. 5. When we are receiving our creature-comforts, we must <hi type="italic">look up to heaven.</hi> Christ did so, to teach us to do so. We must acknowledge that we receive them from God, and that we are unworthy to receive them,—that we owe them all, and all the comfort we have in them, to the mediation of Christ, by whom the curse is removed, and the covenant of peace settled,—that we depend upon God's blessing upon them to make them serviceable to us, and desire that blessing. 6. The blessing of Christ will make a little go a great way. The <hi type="italic">little that the righteous man has is better than the riches of many wicked, a dinner of herbs better than a stalled ox.</hi> 7. Those whom Christ <hi type="italic">feeds</hi> he <hi type="italic">fills;</hi> to whom he gives, he gives enough; as there is in him enough for <hi type="italic">all,</hi> so there is enough for <hi type="italic">each.</hi> He replenishes every hungry soul, abundantly satisfies it with the <hi type="italic">goodness of his house.</hi> Here were <hi type="italic">fragments taken up,</hi> to assure us that in our Father's house there is <hi type="italic">bread enough, and to spare.</hi> We are not straitened, or stinted, in him.
entries.85cc59a970aa2e1af5c85672d8d62021d15b458b: <div eID="gen25658" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Peter's Enlightened Testimony;Self-Denial Enjoined.</title> <div sID="gen25659" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> And it came to pass, as he was alone praying, his disciples were with him: and he asked them, saying, Whom say the people that I am? <hi type="super">19</hi> They answering said, John the Baptist; but some <hi type="italic">say,</hi> Elias; and others <hi type="italic">say,</hi> that one of the old prophets is risen again. <hi type="super">20</hi> He said unto them, But whom say ye that I am? Peter answering said, The Christ of God. <hi type="super">21</hi> And he straitly charged them, and commanded <hi type="italic">them</hi> to tell no man that thing; <hi type="super">22</hi> Saying, The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and be raised the third day. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he said to <hi type="italic">them</hi> all, If any <hi type="italic">man</hi> will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. <hi type="super">24</hi> For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it. <hi type="super">25</hi> For what is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world, and lose himself, or be cast away? <hi type="super">26</hi> For whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he shall come in his own glory, and <hi type="italic">in his</hi> Father's, and of the holy angels. <hi type="super">27</hi> But I tell you of a truth, there be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the kingdom of God. <div eID="gen25659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25660" type="x-p"/> In these verses, we have Christ discoursing with his disciples about the great things that <hi type="italic">pertained to the kingdom of God;</hi> and one circumstance of this discourse is taken notice of here which we had not in the other evangelists-that Christ was <hi type="italic">alone praying,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">disciples with him,</hi> when he entered into this discourse, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.18">v. 18</reference>. Observe, 1. Though Christ had much public work to do, yet he found some time to be <hi type="italic">alone</hi> in private, for converse with himself, with his Father, and with his disciples. 2. When Christ was alone he was <hi type="italic">praying.</hi> It is good for us to improve our solitude for devotion, that, <hi type="italic">when we are alone,</hi> we may <hi type="italic">not be alone,</hi> but may have <hi type="italic">the Father with us.</hi> 3. When Christ was alone, praying, his <hi type="italic">disciples were with him,</hi> to join with him in his prayer; so that this was a family-prayer. Housekeepers ought to pray with their households, parents with their children, masters with their servants, teachers and tutors with their scholars and pupils. 4. Christ <hi type="italic">prayed</hi> with them before he <hi type="italic">examined</hi> them, that they might be directed and encouraged to answer him, by his prayers for them. Those we give instructions to we should put up prayers for and with. He discourses with them, <div eID="gen25660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25661" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning himself; and enquires, <div eID="gen25661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25662" type="x-p"/> 1. What <hi type="italic">the people</hi> said of him: <hi type="italic">Who say the people that I am?</hi> Christ knew better than they did, but would have his disciples made sensible, by the mistakes of others concerning him, how happy they were that were led into the knowledge of him and of the truth concerning him. We should take notice of the ignorance and errors of others, that we may be the more thankful to him who has <hi type="italic">manifested himself to us, and not unto the world,</hi> and may <hi type="italic">pity</hi> them, and do what we can to help them and to teach them better. They tell him what conjectures concerning him they had heard in their converse with the common people. Ministers would know better how to suit their instructions, reproofs, and counsels, to the case of ordinary people, if they did but converse more frequently and familiarly with them; they would then be the better able to say what is proper to rectify their notions, correct their irregularities, and remove their prejudices. The more conversant the physician is with his patient, the better he knows what to do for him. Some said that he was John Baptist, who was beheaded but the other day; others Elias, or <hi type="italic">one of the old prophets;</hi> any thing but what he was. <div eID="gen25662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25663" type="x-p"/> 2. What <hi type="italic">they</hi> said of him. "Now see what an advantage you have by your discipleship; you know better." "So we do," saith Peter, "thanks be to our Master for it; we know that thou art <hi type="italic">the Christ of God,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Anointed</hi> of God, the Messiah promised." It is matter of unspeakable comfort to us that our Lord Jesus is <hi type="italic">God's anointed,</hi> for then he has unquestionable authority and ability for his undertaking; for his being <hi type="italic">anointed</hi> signifies his being both appointed to it and qualified for it. Now one would have expected that Christ should have charged his disciples, who were so fully apprized and assured of this truth, to publish it to every one they met with; but no, he <hi type="italic">strictly charged them to tell no man that thing</hi> as yet, because there is a time for all things. After his resurrection, which completed the proof of it, Peter made the temple ring of it, that <hi type="italic">God had made this same Jesus both Lord and Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.36">Acts ii. 36</reference>); but as yet the evidence was not ready to be summed up, and therefore it must be concealed; while it was so, we may conclude that the belief of it was not necessary to salvation. <div eID="gen25663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25664" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning his own <hi type="italic">sufferings</hi> and <hi type="italic">death,</hi> of which he had yet said little. Now that his disciples were well established in the belief of his being the Christ, and able to bear it, he speaks of them expressly, and with great assurance, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.22">v. 22</reference>. It comes in as a reason why they must not yet preach that he was <hi type="italic">the Christ,</hi> because the wonders that would attend his death and resurrection would be the most convincing proof of his being <hi type="italic">the Christ of God.</hi> It was by his <hi type="italic">exaltation</hi> to the <hi type="italic">right hand of the Father</hi> that he was fully declared to be <hi type="italic">the Christ,</hi> and by the sending of the Spirit thereupon (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.33">Acts ii. 33</reference>); and therefore wait till that is done. <div eID="gen25664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25665" type="x-p"/> III. Concerning their sufferings for him. So far must they be from thinking how to <hi type="italic">prevent</hi> his sufferings that they must rather prepare for their own. <div eID="gen25665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25666" type="x-p"/> 1. We must <hi type="italic">accustom</hi> ourselves to all instances of <hi type="italic">self-denial</hi> and <hi type="italic">patience,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.23">v. 23</reference>. This is the best preparative for martyrdom. We must live a life of self-denial, mortification, and contempt of the world; we must not indulge our ease and appetite, for then it will be hard to bear toil, and weariness, and want, for Christ. We are <hi type="italic">daily</hi> subject to affliction, and we must <hi type="italic">accommodate</hi> ourselves to it, and <hi type="italic">acquiesce</hi> in the will of God in it, and must learn to endure hardship. We frequently meet with crosses in the way of duty; and, though we must not pull them upon our own heads, yet, when they are laid for us, we must <hi type="italic">take them up,</hi> carry them after Christ, and make the best of them. <div eID="gen25666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25667" type="x-p"/> 2. We must <hi type="italic">prefer the salvation and happiness of our souls</hi> before any <hi type="italic">secular concern</hi> whatsoever. Reckon upon it, (1.) That he who to preserve his liberty or estate, his power or preferment, nay, or to save his life, denies Christ and his truths, wilfully wrongs his conscience, and sins against God, will be, not only not a <hi type="italic">saver,</hi> but an unspeakable <hi type="italic">loser,</hi> in the issue, when <hi type="italic">profit</hi> and <hi type="italic">loss</hi> come to be balanced: <hi type="italic">He that will save his life upon these terms will lose it,</hi> will lose that which is of infinitely more value, his precious soul. (2.) We must firmly believe also that, if we lose our life for cleaving to Christ and our religion, we shall <hi type="italic">save</hi> it to our unspeakable advantage; for we shall be abundantly recompensed in the resurrection of the just, when we shall have it again a new and an eternal life. (3.) That the gain of all the world, if we should forsake Christ, and fall in with the interests of the world, would be so far from countervailing the eternal loss and ruin of the soul that it would bear no manner of proportion to it, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.25">v. 25</reference>. If we could be supposed to gain all the wealth, honour, and pleasure, in the world, by denying Christ, yet when, by <hi type="italic">so doing,</hi> we <hi type="italic">lose ourselves</hi> to all eternity, and are <hi type="italic">cast away</hi> at last, what good will our worldly gain do us? Observe, In Matthew and Mark the dreadful issue is a man's <hi type="italic">losing his own soul,</hi> here it is <hi type="italic">losing himself,</hi> which plainly intimates that <hi type="italic">our souls</hi> are <hi type="italic">ourselves. Animus cujusque is est quisque—The soul is the man;</hi> and it is well or ill with us according as it is well or ill with our souls. If they perish for ever, under the weight of their own guilt and corruption, it is certain that <hi type="italic">we</hi> are undone. The body cannot be happy if the soul be miserable in the other world; but the soul may be happy though the body be greatly afflicted and oppressed in this world. If a man be himself <hi type="italic">cast away,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">e zemiotheis</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">if he be damaged,</hi>—or if he be punished, <hi type="italic">si mulctetur—if he have a mulct put upon his soul</hi> by the righteous sentence of Christ, whose cause and interest he has treacherously deserted,—if it be adjudged a forfeiture of all his blessedness, and the forfeiture be taken, where is his gain? What is his hope? <div eID="gen25667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25668" type="x-p"/> 3. We must therefore <hi type="italic">never be ashamed</hi> of Christ and his gospel, nor of any disgrace or reproach that we may undergo for our faithful adherence to him and it, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.26">v. 26</reference>. <hi type="italic">For whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him shall the Son of man be ashamed,</hi> and justly. When the service and honour of Christ called for his testimony and agency, he denied them, because the interest <hi type="italic">of Christ</hi> was a <hi type="italic">despised</hi> interest, and <hi type="italic">every where spoken against;</hi> and therefore he can expect no other than that in the great day, when his case calls for Christ's appearance on his behalf, Christ will be ashamed to own such a cowardly, worldly, sneaking spirit, and will say, "He is none of mine; he belongs not to me." As Christ had a state of <hi type="italic">humiliation</hi> and of <hi type="italic">exaltation,</hi> so likewise has his cause. They, and they only, that are willing to suffer with it when it suffers, shall reign with it when it reigns; but those that cannot find in their hearts to share with it in its <hi type="italic">disgrace,</hi> and to say, <hi type="italic">If this be to be vile, I will be yet more vile,</hi> shall certainly have no share with it in its <hi type="italic">triumphs.</hi> Observe here, How Christ, to support himself and his followers under present disgraces, speaks <hi type="italic">magnificently</hi> of the lustre of his second coming, in prospect of which he <hi type="italic">endured the cross, despising the shame.</hi> (1.) He shall come <hi type="italic">in his own glory.</hi> This was not mentioned in Matthew and Mark. He shall come in the glory of the Mediator, <hi type="italic">all the glory</hi> which the Father <hi type="italic">restored to him,</hi> which he had with God before the worlds were, which he had <hi type="italic">deposited</hi> and <hi type="italic">put in pledge,</hi> as it were, for the accomplishing of his undertaking, and demanded again when he had gone through it. <hi type="italic">Now, O Father, glorify thou me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.4-John.17.5">John xvii. 4, 5</reference>. He shall come in <hi type="italic">all that glory</hi> which the Father <hi type="italic">conferred upon him</hi> when <hi type="italic">he set him at his own right hand,</hi> and <hi type="italic">gave him to be head over all things to the church;</hi> in all the glory that is due to him as the assertor of the glory of God, and the author of the glory of all the saints. This is <hi type="italic">his own glory.</hi> (2.) He shall come <hi type="italic">in his Father's glory.</hi> The Father will judge the world by him, having committed all judgment to him; and therefore will publicly own him in the judgment as the <hi type="italic">brightness of his glory</hi> and the <hi type="italic">express image</hi> of his person. (3.) He shall come in <hi type="italic">the glory of the holy angels.</hi> They shall all <hi type="italic">attend</hi> him, and <hi type="italic">minister</hi> to him, and add every thing they can to the lustre of his appearance. What a figure will the blessed Jesus make in that day! Did we believe it, we should never be ashamed of him or his words now. <div eID="gen25668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25669" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> To encourage them in suffering for him, he assures them that <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God</hi> would now <hi type="italic">shortly be set up,</hi> notwithstanding the great opposition that was made to it, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.27">v. 27</reference>. "Though the second coming of the Son of man is at a great distance, the kingdom of God shall come in its power in the present age, while some here present are alive." They <hi type="italic">saw the kingdom of God</hi> when the Spirit was poured out, when the gospel was preached to all the world and nations were brought to Christ by it; they saw the kingdom of God triumph over the Gentile nations in their <hi type="italic">conversion,</hi> and over the Jewish nation in its <hi type="italic">destruction.</hi>
entries.8e05b4b56d33cd5879582028675de299804db299: <div eID="gen25669" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Transfiguration.</title> <div sID="gen25670" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> And it came to pass about an eight days after these sayings, he took Peter and John and James, and went up into a mountain to pray. <hi type="super">29</hi> And as he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered, and his raiment <hi type="italic">was</hi> white <hi type="italic">and</hi> glistering. <hi type="super">30</hi> And, behold, there talked with him two men, which were Moses and Elias: <hi type="super">31</hi> Who appeared in glory, and spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem. <hi type="super">32</hi> But Peter and they that were with him were heavy with sleep: and when they were awake, they saw his glory, and the two men that stood with him. <hi type="super">33</hi> And it came to pass, as they departed from him, Peter said unto Jesus, Master, it is good for us to be here: and let us make three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias: not knowing what he said. 34 While he thus spake, there came a cloud, and overshadowed them: and they feared as they entered into the cloud. <hi type="super">35</hi> And there came a voice out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son: hear him. <hi type="super">36</hi> And when the voice was past, Jesus was found alone. And they kept <hi type="italic">it</hi> close, and told no man in those days any of those things which they had seen. <div eID="gen25670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25671" type="x-p"/> We have here the narrative of Christ's transfiguration, which was designed for a specimen of that glory of his in which he will come to judge the world, of which he had lately been speaking, and, consequently, an encouragement to his disciples to suffer for him, and never to be ashamed of him. We had this account before in Matthew and Mark, and it is well worthy to be repeated to us, and reconsidered by us, for the <hi type="italic">confirmation of our faith</hi> in the Lord Jesus, as <hi type="italic">the brightness of his Father's glory</hi> and the light of the world, for the <hi type="italic">filling</hi> of our minds with <hi type="italic">high</hi> and <hi type="italic">honourable</hi> thoughts of him, notwithstanding his being clothed with a body, and <hi type="italic">giving</hi> us <hi type="italic">some idea</hi> of the <hi type="italic">glory</hi> which he entered into at his <hi type="italic">ascension,</hi> and in which he now <hi type="italic">appears</hi> within the veil, and for the <hi type="italic">raising</hi> and <hi type="italic">encouraging</hi> of our <hi type="italic">hopes</hi> and <hi type="italic">expectations</hi> concerning the glory reserved for all believers in the future state. <div eID="gen25671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25672" type="x-p"/> I. Here is one circumstance of the narrative that seems to differ from the other two evangelists that related it. They said that it was <hi type="italic">six days</hi> after the foregoing sayings; Luke says that it was <hi type="italic">about eight days after,</hi> that is, it was that day sevennight, six whole days intervening, and it was the eighth day. Some think that it was <hi type="italic">in the night</hi> that Christ was transfigured, because the disciples were sleepy, as in his agony, and <hi type="italic">in the night</hi> his appearance in splendour would be the more illustrious; if in the night, the computation of the time would be the more doubtful and uncertain; probably, in the night, between the seventh and eighth day, and so about eight days. <div eID="gen25672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25673" type="x-p"/> II. Here are divers circumstances added and explained, which are very material. <div eID="gen25673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25674" type="x-p"/> 1. We are <hi type="italic">here</hi> told that Christ had this honour put upon him when he was <hi type="italic">praying:</hi> He <hi type="italic">went up into a mountain to pray,</hi> as he frequently did (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.28">v. 28</reference>), and <hi type="italic">as he prayed</hi> he was <hi type="italic">transfigured.</hi> When Christ <hi type="italic">humbled</hi> himself to pray, he was thus <hi type="italic">exalted.</hi> He knew before that this was designed for him at this time, and therefore seeks it by prayer. Christ himself must <hi type="italic">sue out</hi> the favours that were purposed for him, and promised to him: <hi type="italic">Ask of me, and I will give thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 8</reference>. And thus he intended to put an <hi type="italic">honour</hi> upon the duty of prayer, and to <hi type="italic">recommend</hi> it to us. It is a transfiguring, transforming duty; if our hearts be elevated and enlarged in it, so as in it to <hi type="italic">behold the glory of the Lord,</hi> we shall be <hi type="italic">changed into the same image from glory to glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. By prayer we fetch in the wisdom, grace, and joy, which <hi type="italic">make the face to shine.</hi> <div eID="gen25674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25675" type="x-p"/> 2. Luke does not use the word <hi type="italic">transfigured</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">metamorphothe</hi></hi> (which Matthew and Mark used), perhaps because it had been used so much in the Pagan theology, but makes use of a phrase equivalent, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">to eidos tou prosopou heteron</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the fashion of his countenance was another thing from what it had been:</hi> his face shone far beyond what Moses's did when he came down from the mount; and <hi type="italic">his raiment</hi> was <hi type="italic">white and glistering:</hi> it was <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">exastrapton</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">bright like lightning</hi> (a word used only here), so that he seemed to be arrayed all with light, to <hi type="italic">cover himself with light as with a garment.</hi> <div eID="gen25675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25676" type="x-p"/> 3. It was said in Matthew and Mark that Moses and Elias <hi type="italic">appeared to them;</hi> here it is said that they <hi type="italic">appeared in glory,</hi> to teach us that saints departed are <hi type="italic">in glory,</hi> are in a <hi type="italic">glorious</hi> state; they shine in glory. He being in glory, they <hi type="italic">appeared with him in glory,</hi> as all the saints shall shortly do. <div eID="gen25676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25677" type="x-p"/> 4. We are here told what was the subject of the discourse between Christ and the two great prophets of the Old Testament: <hi type="italic">They spoke of his decease, which he should accomplish at Jerusalem.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Elegon ten exodon autou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">his exodus, his departure;</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">his death.</hi> (1.) The death of Christ is here called his <hi type="italic">exit,</hi> his <hi type="italic">going out,</hi> his <hi type="italic">leaving the world.</hi> Moses and Elias spoke of it to him under that notion, to reconcile him to it, and to make the foresight of it the more easy to his human nature. The death of the saints is their <hi type="italic">exodus,</hi> their departure out of the Egypt of this world, their release out of a <hi type="italic">house of bondage.</hi> Some think that the ascension of Christ is included here in his departure; for the departure of Israel out of Egypt was a departure in <hi type="italic">triumph,</hi> so was <hi type="italic">his</hi> when he went from earth to heaven. (2.) This departure of his he <hi type="italic">must accomplish;</hi> for thus it was determined, the matter was immutably fixed in the counsel of God, and could not be altered. (3.) He must accomplish it at Jerusalem, though his residence was mostly in Galilee; for his most spiteful enemies were at Jerusalem, and there the sanhedrim sat, that took upon them to judge of prophets. (4.) Moses and Elias spoke of this, to intimate that the <hi type="italic">sufferings</hi> of Christ, and his <hi type="italic">entrance into his glory,</hi> were what Moses and <hi type="italic">the prophets</hi> had <hi type="italic">spoken of;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Luke.24.26-Luke.24.27">Luke xxiv. 26, 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>. (5.) Our Lord Jesus, even in his transfiguration, was willing to enter into a discourse concerning his death and sufferings, to teach us that meditations on death, as it is our departure out of this world to another, are never unseasonable, but in a special manner season able when at any time we are <hi type="italic">advanced,</hi> lest we should be <hi type="italic">lifted up above measure.</hi> In our greatest glories on earth, let us remember that here <hi type="italic">we have no continuing city.</hi> <div eID="gen25677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25678" type="x-p"/> 5. We are here told, which we were not before, that the disciples were <hi type="italic">heavy with sleep,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.32">v. 32</reference>. When the vision first began, Peter, and James, and John were drowsy, and inclined to sleep. Either it was late, or they were weary, or had been disturbed in their rest the night before; or perhaps a charming composing air, or some sweet and melodious sounds, which disposed them to soft and gentle slumbers, were a preface to the vision; or perhaps it was owing to a sinful carelessness: when Christ was at prayer with them, they did not regard his prayer as they should have done, and, to punish them for that, they were left to <hi type="italic">sleep on now,</hi> when he began to be <hi type="italic">transfigured,</hi> and so lost an opportunity of seeing how that work of wonder was wrought. These three were now asleep, when Christ was in <hi type="italic">his glory,</hi> as afterwards they were, when he was in <hi type="italic">his agony;</hi> see the <hi type="italic">weakness</hi> and <hi type="italic">frailty</hi> of human nature, even in the best, and what need they have of the grace of God. Nothing could be more affecting to these disciples, one would think, than the <hi type="italic">glories</hi> and the <hi type="italic">agonies</hi> of their Master, and both in the highest degree; and yet neither the one nor the other would serve to <hi type="italic">keep them awake.</hi> What need have we to pray to God for quickening grace, to make us not only <hi type="italic">alive,</hi> but <hi type="italic">lively!</hi> Yet that they might be competent witnesses of <hi type="italic">this sign from heaven,</hi> to those that demanded one, after awhile they <hi type="italic">recovered themselves,</hi> and became perfectly awake; and then they took an exact view of all those glories, so that they were able to give a particular account, as we find one of them does, of all that passed when they were with Christ <hi type="italic">in the holy mount,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.18">2 Pet. i. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen25678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25679" type="x-p"/> 6. It is here observed that it was when Moses and Elias were now about to <hi type="italic">depart</hi> that Peter said, <hi type="italic">Lord, it is good to be here, let us make three tabernacles.</hi> Thus we are often not sensible of the worth of our mercies till we are about to lose them; nor do we covet and court their continuance till they are upon the departure. Peter said this, <hi type="italic">not knowing what he said.</hi> Those know not what they say that talk of making tabernacles on earth for glorified saints in heaven, who have better mansions in the temple there, and long to return to them. <div eID="gen25679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25680" type="x-p"/> 7. It is here added, concerning the <hi type="italic">cloud</hi> that <hi type="italic">overshadowed them,</hi> that they <hi type="italic">feared as they entered into the cloud.</hi> This cloud was a token of God's more peculiar presence. It was in a cloud that God of old took possession of the tabernacle and temple, and, when the cloud <hi type="italic">covered the tabernacle, Moses was not able to enter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.40.34-Exod.40.35">Exod. xl. 34, 35</reference>), and, when it filled the temple, the <hi type="italic">priests could not stand to minister by reason of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.14">2 Chron. v. 14</reference>. Such a cloud was this, and then no wonder that the disciples were <hi type="italic">afraid to enter into it.</hi> But never let any be afraid to enter into a cloud with Jesus Christ; for he will be sure to bring them safely through it. <div eID="gen25680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25681" type="x-p"/> 8. The <hi type="italic">voice</hi> which came from heaven is here, and in Mark, related not so fully as in Matthew: <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son, hear him:</hi> though those words, <hi type="italic">in whom I am well pleased,</hi> which we have both in Matthew and Peter, are not expressed, they are implied in that, <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son;</hi> for whom he <hi type="italic">loves,</hi> and in whom he is <hi type="italic">well pleased,</hi> come all to one; we are <hi type="italic">accepted in the Beloved.</hi> <div eID="gen25681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25682" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The apostles are here said to have kept this vision private. They <hi type="italic">told no man in those days,</hi> reserving the discovery of it for another opportunity, when the evidences of Christ's being the Son of God were completed in the pouring out of the Spirit, and that doctrine was to be published to all the world. As there is a time <hi type="italic">to speak,</hi> so there is a time to <hi type="italic">keep silence.</hi> Every thing is beautiful and useful in its season.
entries.8948020c5c5b999b0d4c84ec0cf66286f444f741: <div eID="gen25682" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">An Evil Spirit Expelled.</title> <div sID="gen25683" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">37</hi> And it came to pass, that on the next day, when they were come down from the hill, much people met him. <hi type="super">38</hi> And, behold, a man of the company cried out, saying, Master, I beseech thee, look upon my son: for he is mine only child. <hi type="super">39</hi> And, lo, a spirit taketh him, and he suddenly crieth out; and it teareth him that he foameth again, and bruising him hardly departeth from him. <hi type="super">40</hi> And I besought thy disciples to cast him out; and they could not. <hi type="super">41</hi> And Jesus answering said, O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you, and suffer you? Bring thy son hither. <hi type="super">42</hi> And as he was yet a coming, the devil threw him down, and tare <hi type="italic">him.</hi> And Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, and healed the child, and delivered him again to his father. <div eID="gen25683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25684" type="x-p"/> This passage of story in Matthew and Mark follows immediately upon that of Christ's transfiguration, and his discourse with his disciples after it; but here it is said to be <hi type="italic">on the next day, as they were coming down from the hill,</hi> which confirms the conjecture that Christ was transfigured <hi type="italic">in the night,</hi> and, it should seem, though they did not <hi type="italic">make tabernacles</hi> as Peter proposed, yet they found some shelter to repose themselves in all night, for it was not till next day that they <hi type="italic">came down from the hill,</hi> and then he found things in some disorder among his disciples, though not so bad as Moses did when he came down from the mount. When wise and good men are in their beloved retirements, they would do well to consider whether they are not wanted in their <hi type="italic">public stations.</hi> <div eID="gen25684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25685" type="x-p"/> In this narrative here, observe, 1. How forward the people were to receive Christ at his return to them. Though he had been but a little while absent, <hi type="italic">much people met him,</hi> as, at other times, much people <hi type="italic">followed</hi> him; for so it was foretold concerning him, that <hi type="italic">to him should the gathering of the people be.</hi> 2. How importunate the father of the lunatic child was with Christ for help for him (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">I beseech thee, look upon my son;</hi> this is his request, and it is a very modest one; one compassionate look from Christ is enough to set every thing to rights. Let us bring ourselves and our children to Christ, to be <hi type="italic">looked upon.</hi> His plea is, <hi type="italic">He is my only child.</hi> They that have many children may balance their affliction in one with their comfort in the rest; yet, if it be an only child that is a grief, the affliction in that may be balanced with the love of God in giving his only-begotten Son for us. 3. How <hi type="italic">deplorable</hi> the case of the <hi type="italic">child</hi> was, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.39">v. 39</reference>. He was under the power of an evil spirit, that <hi type="italic">took him;</hi> and diseases of that nature are more frightful than such as arise merely from natural causes: when the fit seized him without any warning given, he suddenly <hi type="italic">cried out,</hi> and many a time his shrieks had pierced the heart of his tender father. This malicious spirit <hi type="italic">tore him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">bruised</hi> him, and <hi type="italic">departed not from him</hi> but with great difficulty, and a deadly gripe at parting. O the afflictions of the afflicted in this world! And what mischief doth Satan do where he gets possession! But happy they that have access to Christ! 4. How defective the disciples were in their faith. Though Christ had given them <hi type="italic">power over unclean spirits,</hi> yet they <hi type="italic">could not</hi> cast out this <hi type="italic">evil spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.40">v. 40</reference>. Either they distrusted the power they were to fetch in strength from, or the commission given to them, or they did not exert themselves in prayer as they ought; for this Christ reproved them. O <hi type="italic">faithless and perverse generation.</hi> Dr. Clarke understands this as spoken to his disciples: "<hi type="italic">Will ye be</hi> yet so faithless and full of distrust that ye cannot execute the commission I have given you?" 5. How effectual the cure was, which Christ wrought upon this child, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.42">v. 42</reference>. Christ can do that for us which his disciples cannot: <hi type="italic">Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit</hi> then when he raged most. The devil <hi type="italic">threw the child down, and tore him,</hi> distorted him, as if he would have pulled him to pieces. But one word from Christ <hi type="italic">healed the child,</hi> and made good the damage the devil had done him. And it is here added that he <hi type="italic">delivered him again to his father.</hi> Note, When our children are recovered from sickness, we must receive them as delivered to us again, receive them as life from the dead, and as when we first received them. It is comfortable to receive them from the hand of Christ, to see him delivering them to us again: "Here, take this child, and be thankful; take it, and bring it up for me, for thou hast it again from me. Take it, and do not set thy heart too much upon it." With such cautions as these, parents should receive their children <hi type="italic">from Christ's hands,</hi> and then with comfort put them again <hi type="italic">into his hands.</hi>
entries.2ceff4794acdafe870c8d4c4df2841ffd7825792: <div eID="gen25685" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ambition of the Disciples Reproved.</title> <div sID="gen25686" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">43</hi> And they were all amazed at the mighty power of God. But while they wondered every one at all things which Jesus did, he said unto his disciples, <hi type="super">44</hi> Let these sayings sink down into your ears: for the Son of man shall be delivered into the hands of men. <hi type="super">45</hi> But they understood not this saying, and it was hid from them, that they perceived it not: and they feared to ask him of that saying. <hi type="super">46</hi> Then there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest. <hi type="super">47</hi> And Jesus, perceiving the thought of their heart, took a child, and set him by him, <hi type="super">48</hi> And said unto them, Whosoever shall receive this child in my name receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me receiveth him that sent me: for he that is least among you all, the same shall be great. <hi type="super">49</hi> And John answered and said, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name; and we forbad him, because he followeth not with us. <hi type="super">50</hi> And Jesus said unto him, Forbid <hi type="italic">him</hi> not: for he that is not against us is for us. <div eID="gen25686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25687" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, I. The impression which Christ's miracles made upon all that beheld them (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">They were all amazed at the mighty power of God,</hi> which they could not but see in all the miracles Christ wrought. Note, The works of God's almighty power are amazing, especially those that are wrought by the hand of the Lord Jesus; for he is <hi type="italic">the power of God,</hi> and his name is <hi type="italic">Wonderful.</hi> Their wonder was universal: they wondered <hi type="italic">every one.</hi> The causes of it were universal: they wondered at <hi type="italic">all things which Jesus did;</hi> all his actions had something uncommon and surprising in them. <div eID="gen25687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25688" type="x-p"/> II. The notice Christ gave to his disciples of his approaching sufferings: <hi type="italic">The Son of man shall be delivered into the hands of men,</hi> wicked men, men of the worst character; they shall be permitted to abuse him at their pleasure. That is here <hi type="italic">implied</hi> which is <hi type="italic">expressed</hi> by the other evangelists: <hi type="italic">They shall kill him.</hi> But that which is peculiar here is, 1. The connection of this with what goes next before, of the admiration with which the people were struck at beholding Christ's miracles (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">While they all wondered at all things which Jesus did, he said this to his disciples.</hi> They had a fond conceit of his temporal kingdom, and that he should reign, and they with him, in secular pomp and power; and now they thought that this <hi type="italic">mighty power</hi> of his would easily effect the thing, and his interest gained by his miracles in the people would contribute to it; and therefore Christ, who knew what was in their hearts, takes this occasion to tell them again, what he had told them before, that he was so far from having men <hi type="italic">delivered into his hands</hi> that he must be <hi type="italic">delivered into the hands of men,</hi> so far from living in honour that he must die in disgrace; and all his miracles, and the interest he has by them gained in the hearts of the people, will not be able to prevent it. 2. The solemn preface with which it is introduced: "<hi type="italic">Let these sayings sink down into your ears;</hi> take special notice of what I say, and mix faith with it; let not the notions you have of the temporal kingdom of the Messiah stop your ears against it, nor make you unwilling to believe it. Admit what I say, and submit to it." <hi type="italic">Let it sink down into your hearts;</hi> so the Syriac and Arabic read it. The word of Christ does us no good, unless we let it sink down into our heads and hearts. 3. The unaccountable stupidity of the disciples, with reference to this prediction of Christ's sufferings. It was said in Mark, <hi type="italic">They understood not that saying.</hi> It was plain enough, but they <hi type="italic">would not</hi> understand it in the literal sense, because it agreed not with their notions; and they <hi type="italic">could not</hi> understand it in any other, <hi type="italic">and were afraid to ask him</hi> lest they should be undeceived and awaked out of their pleasing dream. But it is here added that <hi type="italic">it was hidden from them, that they perceived it not,</hi> through the weakness of faith and the power of prejudice. We cannot think that it was <hi type="italic">in mercy</hi> hidden from them, lest they should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow at the prospect of it; but that it was a paradox, because they <hi type="italic">made it so</hi> to themselves. <div eID="gen25688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25689" type="x-p"/> III. The rebuke Christ gave to his disciples for their disputing among themselves which should be greatest, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.46-Luke.9.48">v. 46-48</reference>. This passage we had before, and, the more is the pity, we shall meet with the like again. Observe here, <div eID="gen25689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25690" type="x-p"/> 1. Ambition of honour, and strife for superiority and precedency, are sins that most easily beset the disciples of our Lord Jesus, for which they deserve to be severely rebuked; they flow from corruptions which they are highly concerned to subdue and mortify, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.46">v. 46</reference>. They that expect to be <hi type="italic">great</hi> in this world commonly aim high, and nothing will serve them short of being <hi type="italic">greatest;</hi> this exposes them to a great deal of temptation and trouble, which they are safe from that are content to be <hi type="italic">little,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">least,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">less than the least.</hi> <div eID="gen25690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25691" type="x-p"/> 2. Jesus Christ is perfectly acquainted with the thoughts and intents of our hearts: He <hi type="italic">perceived their thoughts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.47">v. 47</reference>. Thoughts are <hi type="italic">words</hi> to him, and <hi type="italic">whispers</hi> are loud cries. It is a good reason why we should keep up a strict government of our thoughts because Christ takes a strict cognizance of them. <div eID="gen25691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25692" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ will have his disciples to aim at that honour which is to be obtained by a quiet and condescending humility, and not at that which is to be obtained by a restless and aspiring ambition. Christ <hi type="italic">took a child, and set him by him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.47">v. 47</reference> (for he always expressed a tenderness and kindness for little children), and he proposed <hi type="italic">this child</hi> to them for an example. (1.) Let them be of the <hi type="italic">temper</hi> of this child, <hi type="italic">humble</hi> and <hi type="italic">quiet,</hi> and <hi type="italic">easy</hi> to itself; let them not affect worldly pomp, or grandeur, or high titles, but be as dead to them as this child; let them bear no more malice to their rivals and competitors than this child did. Let them be willing to be <hi type="italic">the least,</hi> if that would contribute any thing to their usefulness, to stoop to the meanest office whereby they might <hi type="italic">do good.</hi> (2.) Let them assure themselves that this was the way to preferment; for this would recommend them to the esteem of their brethren: they that loved Christ would <hi type="italic">therefore receive</hi> them <hi type="italic">in his name,</hi> because they did most resemble him, and they would likewise recommend themselves to his favour, for Christ would take the kindnesses done to them as done to himself: <hi type="italic">Whosoever shall receive one such child,</hi> a preacher of the gospel that is of such a disposition as this, he placeth his respect aright, and <hi type="italic">receiveth me;</hi> and <hi type="italic">whosoever receiveth me,</hi> in such a minister, <hi type="italic">receiveth him that sent me;</hi> and what greater honour can any man attain to in this world than to be received by men as a messenger of God and Christ, and to have God and Christ own themselves received and welcomed in him? This honour have all the humble disciples of Jesus Christ, and thus they shall be truly great that are least among them. <div eID="gen25692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25693" type="x-p"/> IV. The rebuke Christ gave to his disciples for discouraging one that honoured him and served him, but was not of their communion, not only not one of the twelve, nor one of the seventy, but not one of those that ever associated with them, or attended on them, but, upon occasional hearing of Christ, believed in him, and made use of his name with faith and prayer in a serious manner, for the casting out of devils. Now, 1. This man they <hi type="italic">rebuked and restrained;</hi> they would not let him pray and preach, though it was to the honour of Christ, though it did good to men and weakened Satan's kingdom, because he did not <hi type="italic">follow Christ with them;</hi> he separated from their church, was not ordained as they were, paid them no respect, nor gave them the right hand of fellowship. Now, if ever any society of Christians in this world had reason to silence those that were not of their communion, the twelve disciples at this time had; and yet, 2. Jesus Christ chid them for what they did, and warned them not to do the like again, nor any that profess to be successors of the apostles: "<hi type="italic">Forbid him not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.50">v. 50</reference>), but rather encourage him, for he is carrying on the same design that you are, though, for reasons best known to himself, he does not follow <hi type="italic">with you;</hi> and he will meet you in <hi type="italic">the same end,</hi> though he does not accompany you in <hi type="italic">the same way.</hi> You <hi type="italic">do well</hi> to do as you do, but it does not therefore follow that he <hi type="italic">does ill</hi> to do as he does, and that you do well to put him under an interdict, for <hi type="italic">he that is not against us is for us,</hi> and therefore ought to be countenanced by us." We need not lose any of our friends, while we have so few, and so many enemies. Those may be found faithful followers of Christ, and, as such, may be accepted of him, though they do not follow <hi type="italic">with us.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Mark.9.38-Mark.9.39">Mark ix. 38, 39</reference>. O what a great deal of mischief to the church, even from those that boast of relation to Christ, and pretend to <hi type="italic">envy for his sake,</hi> would be prevented, if this passage of story were but duly considered!
entries.8a976508aa7c6739ba718121c4791409576f77b7: <div eID="gen25693" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Samaritans Refuse to Receive Christ; Mistaken Zeal of James and John.</title> <div sID="gen25694" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">51</hi> And it came to pass, when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem, <hi type="super">52</hi> And sent messengers before his face: and they went, and entered into a village of the Samaritans, to make ready for him. <hi type="super">53</hi> And they did not receive him, because his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">54</hi> And when his disciples James and John saw <hi type="italic">this,</hi> they said, Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did? <hi type="super">55</hi> But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. <hi type="super">56</hi> For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save <hi type="italic">them.</hi> And they went to another village. <div eID="gen25694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25695" type="x-p"/> This passage of story we have not in any other of the evangelists, and it seems to come in here for the sake of its affinity with that next before, for in this also Christ rebuked his disciples, because they envied for his sake. There, under colour of zeal for Christ, they were for silencing and restraining separatists: here, under the same colour, they were for putting infidels to death; and, as for <hi type="italic">that,</hi> so for <hi type="italic">this</hi> also, Christ reprimanded them, for a spirit of bigotry and persecution is directly contrary to the spirit of Christ and Christianity. Observe here, <div eID="gen25695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25696" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">readiness</hi> and <hi type="italic">resolution</hi> of our Lord Jesus, in prosecuting his great undertaking for our redemption and salvation. Of this we have an instance, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.51">v. 51</reference>: <hi type="italic">When the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem.</hi> Observe 1. There was a time fixed for the sufferings and death of our Lord Jesus, and he knew well enough when it was, and had a clear and certain foresight of it, and yet was so far from keeping out of the way that then he appeared most publicly of all, and was most busy, knowing that his time was short. 2. When he saw his death and sufferings approaching, he looked through them and beyond them, to the glory that should follow; he looked upon it as the time when he should be <hi type="italic">received up into glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1 Tim. iii. 16</reference>), received up into the highest heavens, to be enthroned there. Moses and Elias spoke of his death as his departure out of this world, which made it not <hi type="italic">formidable;</hi> but he went further, and looked upon it as his translation to a better world, which made it very <hi type="italic">desirable.</hi> All good Christians may frame to themselves the same notion of death, and may call it their being <hi type="italic">received up,</hi> to be with Christ where he is; and, when the <hi type="italic">time</hi> of their being <hi type="italic">received up</hi> is at hand, let them lift up their heads, knowing that <hi type="italic">their redemption draws nigh.</hi> 3. On this prospect of the joy set before him, he <hi type="italic">stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem</hi> the place where he was to suffer and die. He was fully <hi type="italic">determined</hi> to go, and would not be dissuaded; he went <hi type="italic">directly</hi> to Jerusalem, because there now his business lay, and he did not go about to other towns, or fetch a compass, which if he had done, as commonly he did, he might have avoided going through Samaria. He went cheerfully and courageously thither, though he knew the things that should befal him there. He <hi type="italic">did not fail nor was discouraged,</hi> but <hi type="italic">set his face as a flint, knowing</hi> that he should be not only <hi type="italic">justified,</hi> but glorified (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Isa. l. 7</reference>), not only not <hi type="italic">run down,</hi> but <hi type="italic">received up.</hi> How should this shame us <hi type="italic">for,</hi> and shame <hi type="italic">us out of,</hi> our backwardness to do and suffer for Christ! We draw back, and turn our faces another way from his service who stedfastly set his face against all opposition, to go through with the work of our salvation. <div eID="gen25696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25697" type="x-p"/> II. The <hi type="italic">rudeness</hi> of the Samaritans in a <hi type="italic">certain village</hi> (not named, nor deserving to be so) who would not <hi type="italic">receive him,</hi> nor suffer him to bait in their town, though his way lay through it. Observe here, 1. How <hi type="italic">civil</hi> he was to them: <hi type="italic">He sent messengers before his face,</hi> some of his disciples, that went to take up lodgings, and to know whether he might have leave to accommodate himself and his company among them; for he would not come to give <hi type="italic">offence,</hi> or if they took any umbrage at the number of his followers. He sent some to <hi type="italic">make ready</hi> for him, not for state, but convenience, and that his coming might be no surprise. 2. How <hi type="italic">uncivil</hi> they were to him, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.53">v. 53</reference>. They did not <hi type="italic">receive him,</hi> would not suffer him to come into their village, but ordered their watch to keep him out. He would have <hi type="italic">paid</hi> for all he <hi type="italic">bespoke,</hi> and been a generous guest among them, would have done them good, and preached the gospel to them, as he had done some time ago to another city of the Samaritans, <reference osisRef="John.4.41">John iv. 41</reference>. He would have been, if they pleased, the greatest blessing that ever came to their village, and yet they forbid him entrance. Such treatment his gospel and ministers have often met with. Now the reason was <hi type="italic">because his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem;</hi> they observed, by his motions, that he was steering his course that way. The great controversy between the Jews and the Samaritans was about the place of worship—whether Jerusalem or mount Gerizim near Sychar; see <reference osisRef="John.4.20">John iv. 20</reference>. And so hot was the controversy between them that the <hi type="italic">Jews would have no dealings with the Samaritans,</hi> nor they with them, <reference osisRef="John.4.9">John iv. 9</reference>. Yet we may suppose that they did not deny other Jews lodgings among them, no, not when they went up to the feast; for if that had been their constant practice Christ would not have attempted it, and it would have been a great way about for some of the Galileans to go to Jerusalem any other way than through Samaria. But they were particularly incensed against Christ, who was a celebrated teacher, for owning and adhering to the temple at Jerusalem, when the priests of that temple were such bitter enemies to him, which, they hoped, would have driven him to come and worship at <hi type="italic">their</hi> temple, and bring that into reputation; but when they saw that he would go forward to Jerusalem, notwithstanding this, they would not show him the common civility which probably they used formerly to show him in his journey thither. <div eID="gen25697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25698" type="x-p"/> III. The <hi type="italic">resentment</hi> which James and John expressed of this affront, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.54">v. 54</reference>. When these two heard this message brought, they were all in a flame presently, and nothing will serve them but Sodom's doom upon this village: "Lord," say they, "give us leave to command fire to come down from heaven, not to <hi type="italic">frighten</hi> them only, but to <hi type="italic">consume</hi> them." <div eID="gen25698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25699" type="x-p"/> 1. Here indeed was something commendable, for they showed, (1.) A great confidence in the power they had received from Jesus Christ; though this had not been particularly mentioned in their commission, yet they could with a word's speaking fetch <hi type="italic">fire from heaven.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Theleis eipomen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Wilt thou that we speak the word,</hi> and the thing will be done. (2.) A great zeal for the honour of their Master. They took it very ill that he who did good wherever he came and found a hearty welcome should be denied the liberty of the road by a parcel of paltry Samaritans; they could not think of it without indignation that their Master should be thus slighted. (3.) A submission, notwithstanding, to their Master's good will and pleasure. They will not offer to do such a thing, unless Christ give leave: <hi type="italic">Wilt thou</hi> that we do it? (4.) A regard to the examples of the prophets that were before them. It is doing <hi type="italic">as Elias did?</hi> they would not have thought of such a thing if Elijah had not done it upon the soldiers that came to take him, once and again, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.10">2 Kings i. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.12">12</reference>. They thought that this <hi type="italic">precedent</hi> would be their <hi type="italic">warrant;</hi> so apt are we to misapply the examples of good men, and to think to justify ourselves by them in the irregular liberties we give ourselves, when the case is not parallel. <div eID="gen25699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25700" type="x-p"/> 2. But though there was something right in what they said, yet there was much more amiss, for (1.) This was not the first time, by a great many, that our Lord Jesus had been thus affronted, witness the Nazarenes thrusting him out of their city, and the Gadarenes desiring him to depart out of their coast; and yet he never called for any judgment upon them, but patiently put up with the injury. (2.) These were Samaritans, from whom better was not to be expected, and perhaps they had heard that Christ had forbidden his disciples to <hi type="italic">enter into any of the cities of the Samaritans</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.5">Matt. x. 5</reference>), and therefore it was not so bad in them as in others who knew more of Christ, and had received so many favours from him. (3.) Perhaps it was only some few of the town that knew any thing of the matter, or that sent that rude message to him, while, for aught they knew, there were many in the town who, if they had heard of Christ's being so near them, would have gone to meet him and welcomed him; and must the whole town be laid in ashes for the wickedness of a few? Will they have the righteous destroyed with the wicked? (4.) Their Master had never yet upon any occasion called for <hi type="italic">fire from heaven,</hi> nay, he had refused to give the Pharisees any <hi type="italic">sign from heaven</hi> when they demanded it (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.1-Matt.16.2">Matt. xvi. 1, 2</reference>); and why should they think to introduce it? James and John were the two disciples whom Christ had called <hi type="italic">Boanerges—sons of thunder</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.17">Mark iii. 17</reference>); and will not that serve them, but they must be <hi type="italic">sons of lightning</hi> too? (5.) The example of Elias did not reach the case. Elijah was sent to display the terrors of the law, and to give proof of that, and to witness as a bold reprover against the idolatries and wickednesses of the court of Ahab, and it was agreeable enough to him to have his commission thus proved; but it is a dispensation of grace that is now to be introduced, to which such a terrible display of divine justice will not be at all agreeable.
