Archbishop Tillotson suggests that their being now near Samaria, where Elijah called for fire from heaven, might help to put it in their heads; perhaps at the very place; but, though the <hi type="italic">place</hi> was the same, the <hi type="italic">times</hi> were altered. <div eID="gen25700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25701" type="x-p"/> IV. The <hi type="italic">reproof</hi> he gave to James and John for their fiery, furious zeal (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.55">v. 55</reference>): He <hi type="italic">turned</hi> with a just displeasure, and <hi type="italic">rebuked them;</hi> for <hi type="italic">as many as he loves he rebukes and chastens,</hi> particularly for what they do, that is irregular and unbecoming them, under colour of zeal for him. <div eID="gen25701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25702" type="x-p"/> 1. He shows them in particular their mistake: <hi type="italic">Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of;</hi> that is, (1.) "You <hi type="italic">are not aware</hi> what an <hi type="italic">evil spirit</hi> and disposition you are of; how much there is of pride, and passion, and personal revenge, covered under this pretence of zeal for your Master." Note, There may be much corruption lurking, nay, and stirring too, in the hearts of good people, and they themselves not be sensible of it. (2.) "You <hi type="italic">do not consider</hi> what a <hi type="italic">good spirit,</hi> directly contrary to this, you <hi type="italic">should be of.</hi> Surely you have yet to learn, though you have been so long learning, what the spirit of Christ and Christianity is. Have you not been taught to <hi type="italic">love your enemies,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">bless them that curse you,</hi> and to call for grace from heaven, not fire from heaven, upon them? You know not how contrary your disposition herein is to that which it was the design of the gospel you should be <hi type="italic">delivered</hi> into. You are not now under the dispensation of bondage, and terror, and death, but under the dispensation of love, and liberty, and grace, which was ushered in with a proclamation of <hi type="italic">peace on earth</hi> and <hi type="italic">good will toward men,</hi> to which you ought to accommodate yourselves, and not by such imprecations as these oppose yourselves." <div eID="gen25702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25703" type="x-p"/> 2. He shows them the general design and tendency of his religion (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.56">v. 56</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Son of man</hi> is not himself come, and therefore does not send you abroad <hi type="italic">to destroy men's lives, but to save them.</hi> He designed to propagate his holy religion by love and sweetness, and every thing that is inviting and endearing, not by fire and sword, and blood and slaughter; by miracles of healing, not by plagues and miracles of destruction, as Israel was brought out of Egypt. Christ came to <hi type="italic">slay</hi> all <hi type="italic">enmities,</hi> not to foster them. Those are certainly destitute of the spirit of the gospel that are for anathematizing and rooting out by violence and persecution all that are not of their mind and way, that cannot in conscience say as they say, and do as they do. Christ came, not only to save men's <hi type="italic">souls,</hi> but to save their <hi type="italic">lives</hi> too—witness the many miracles he wrought for the healing of diseases that would otherwise have been <hi type="italic">mortal,</hi> by which, and a thousand other instances of beneficence, it appears that Christ would have his disciples do good to all, to the utmost of their power, but hurt to none, to draw men into his church with the <hi type="italic">cords of a man and the bands of love,</hi> but not think to drive men into it with a <hi type="italic">rod of violence</hi> or the <hi type="italic">scourge of the tongue.</hi> <div eID="gen25703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25704" type="x-p"/> V. His <hi type="italic">retreat</hi> from this village. Christ would not only not punish them for their rudeness, but would not insist upon his right of travelling the road (which was as free to him as to his neighbours), would not attempt to force his way, but quietly and peaceably <hi type="italic">went to another village,</hi> where they were not so stingy and bigoted, and there refreshed himself, and went on his way. Note, When a stream of opposition is strong, it is wisdom to get out of the way of it, rather than to contend with it. If some be very rude, instead of revenging it, we should try whether others will not be more civil.
entries.1cf2f186dba10ffe623718e6ff998231710b110e: <div eID="gen25704" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Every Thing to Be Left for Christ.</title> <div sID="gen25705" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">57</hi> And it came to pass, that, as they went in the way, a certain <hi type="italic">man</hi> said unto him, Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest. <hi type="super">58</hi> And Jesus said unto him, Foxes have holes, and birds of the air <hi type="italic">have</hi> nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay <hi type="italic">his</hi> head. <hi type="super">59</hi> And he said unto another, Follow me. But he said, Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father. <hi type="super">60</hi> Jesus said unto him, Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God. <hi type="super">61</hi> And another also said, Lord, I will follow thee; but let me first go bid them farewell, which are at home at my house. <hi type="super">62</hi> And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God. <div eID="gen25705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25706" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of three several persons that offered themselves to follow Christ, and the answers that Christ gave to each of them. The two former we had an account of in <reference osisRef="Matt.19.21">Matt. xix. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen25706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25707" type="x-p"/> I. Here is one that is extremely forward to follow Christ immediately, but seems to have been too rash, hasty, and inconsiderate, and not to have set down and counted the cost. <div eID="gen25707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25708" type="x-p"/> 1. He makes Christ a very large promise (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.57">v. 57</reference>): <hi type="italic">As they went in the way,</hi> going up to Jerusalem, where it was expected Christ would first appear in his glory, one said to him, <hi type="italic">Lord, I will follow thee withersoever thou goest.</hi> This must be the resolution of all that will be found Christ's disciples indeed; they <hi type="italic">follow the Lamb whithersoever he goes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 4</reference>), though it be through fire and water, to prisons and deaths. <div eID="gen25708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25709" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ gives him a necessary caution, not to promise himself great things in the world, in following him, but, on the contrary, to count upon poverty and meanness; for <hi type="italic">the Son of man has not where to lay his head.</hi> <div eID="gen25709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25710" type="x-p"/> We may look upon this, (1.) As <hi type="italic">setting forth</hi> the <hi type="italic">very low condition</hi> that our Lord Jesus was in, in this world. He not only wanted the delights and ornaments that great princes usually have, but even such accommodations for mere necessity as the <hi type="italic">foxes</hi> have, and the <hi type="italic">birds of the air.</hi> See what a <hi type="italic">depth of poverty</hi> our Lord Jesus submitted to for us, to increase the worth and merit of his satisfaction, and to purchase for us a larger <hi type="italic">allowance of grace, that we through his poverty might be rich,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2 Cor. viii. 9</reference>. He that made all did not make a dwelling-place for himself, not a house of his own to put his head in, but what he was beholden to others for. He here calls himself the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> a Son of Adam, partaker of flesh and blood. He glories in his condescension towards us, not only to the meanness of our nature, but to the meanest condition in that nature, to testify his love to us, and to teach us a holy contempt of the world and of great things in it, and a continual regard to another world. Christ was thus poor, to sanctify and sweeten poverty to his people; the apostles had not certain dwelling-place (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.11">1 Cor. iv. 11</reference>), which they might the better bear when they knew their Master had not; see <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.11">2 Sam. xi. 11</reference>. We may well be content to fare as Christ did. (2.) As proposing this to the consideration of those who intend to be his disciples. If we mean to follow Christ, we must lay aside the thoughts of great things in the world, and not reckon upon making any thing <hi type="italic">more than heaven</hi> of our religion, as we must resolve not to take up with any thing <hi type="italic">less.</hi> Let us not go about to compound the profession of Christianity with secular advantages; Christ has <hi type="italic">put them asunder,</hi> let us not think of <hi type="italic">joining them together;</hi> on the contrary, we must expect to enter into the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations, must <hi type="italic">deny ourselves,</hi> and <hi type="italic">take up our cross.</hi> Christ tells this man what he must count upon if he followed him, to lie cold and uneasy, to fare hard, and live in contempt; if he could not submit to this, let him not pretend to follow Christ. This word sent him back, for aught that appears; but it will be no discouragement to any that know what there is in Christ and heaven to set in the scale against this. <div eID="gen25710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25711" type="x-p"/> II. Here is another, that seems <hi type="italic">resolved</hi> to follow Christ, but he <hi type="italic">begs a day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.59">v. 59</reference>. To this man Christ first gave the call; he said to him, <hi type="italic">Follow me.</hi> He that proposed the thing of himself fled off when he heard of the difficulties that attended it; but this man to whom Christ gave a call, though he hesitated at first, yet, as it should seem, afterwards yielded; so true was that of Christ, <hi type="italic">You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.16">John xv. 16</reference>. It is not of <hi type="italic">him that willeth,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">of him that runneth</hi> (as that forward spark in the foregoing verses), but of God that showeth mercy, that <hi type="italic">gives</hi> the call, and <hi type="italic">makes</hi> it <hi type="italic">effectual,</hi> as to this man here. Observe, <div eID="gen25711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25712" type="x-p"/> 1. The excuse he made: "<hi type="italic">Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father.</hi> I have an aged father at home, who cannot live long, and will need me while he does live; let me go and attend on him until he is dead, and I have performed my last office of love to him, and then I will do any thing." We may here see three temptations, by which we are in danger of being drawn and kept from following Christ, which therefore we should guard against:—(1.) We are tempted to <hi type="italic">rest</hi> in a <hi type="italic">discipleship at large,</hi> in which we may be <hi type="italic">at a loose end,</hi> and not to come <hi type="italic">close,</hi> and give up ourselves to be <hi type="italic">strict</hi> and <hi type="italic">constant.</hi> (2.) We are tempted to <hi type="italic">defer</hi> the doing of that which we know to be our duty, and to put if off to some other time. When we have got clear of such a care and difficulty, when we have despatched such a business, raised an estate to such a pitch, then we will begin to think of being religious; and so we are cozened out of all our time, by being cozened out of the present time. (3.) We are tempted to think that our duty to our relations will excuse us from our duty to Christ. It is a plausible excuse indeed: "<hi type="italic">Let me go and bury my father,</hi>—let me take care of my family, and provide for my children, and then I will think of serving Christ;" whereas the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof</hi> must be sought ad minded <hi type="italic">in the first place.</hi> <div eID="gen25712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25713" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ's answer to it (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.60">v. 60</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let the dead bury their dead.</hi> Suppose (which is not likely) that there are none but the dead to bury their dead, or none but those who are themselves aged and dying, who are <hi type="italic">as good as dead,</hi> and fit for no other service, yet thou hast other work to do; <hi type="italic">go thou, and preach the kingdom of God.</hi>" Not that Christ would have his followers or his ministers to be <hi type="italic">unnatural;</hi> our religion teaches us to be kind and good in every relation, to <hi type="italic">show piety at home,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">requite our parents.</hi> But we must not make these offices an excuse from our duty to God. If the nearest and dearest relation we have in the world stand in our way to keep us from Christ, it is necessary that we have a zeal that will make us forget <hi type="italic">father and mother,</hi> as Levi did, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deut. xxxiii. 9</reference>. This disciple was called to be a minister, and therefore must not <hi type="italic">entangle himself</hi> with the <hi type="italic">affairs of this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.4">2 Tim. ii. 4</reference>. And it is a rule that, whenever Christ calls to any duty, we must not <hi type="italic">consult with flesh and blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.1.15-Gal.1.16">Gal. i. 15, 16</reference>. No excuses must be admitted against a present obedience to the call of Christ. <div eID="gen25713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25714" type="x-p"/> III. Here is another that is willing to follow Christ, but he must have a <hi type="italic">little time</hi> to <hi type="italic">talk with his friends</hi> about it. <div eID="gen25714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25715" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. His request for a dispensation, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.61">v. 61</reference>. He said, "<hi type="italic">Lord, I will follow thee;</hi> I design no other, I am determined to do it: but <hi type="italic">let me first go bid them farewell that are at home.</hi>" This seemed reasonable; it was what Elisha desired when Elijah called him,<hi type="italic">Let me kiss my father and my mother;</hi> and it was allowed him: but the ministry of the gospel is <hi type="italic">preferable,</hi> and the service of it more urgent than that of the prophets; and therefore here it would not be allowed. Suffer me <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">apotaxasthai tois eis ton oikon mou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Let me go and set in order my household affairs,</hi> and give direction concerning them; so some understand it. Now that which was amiss in this is, (1.) That he looked upon his following Christ as a melancholy, troublesome, dangerous thing; it was to him as if he were <hi type="italic">going to die</hi> and therefore he must take <hi type="italic">leave</hi> of all his friends, never to <hi type="italic">see them again,</hi> or never <hi type="italic">with any comfort;</hi> whereas, in following Christ, he might be more a comfort and blessing to them than if he had continued with them. (2.) That he seemed to have his worldly concerns more upon his heart than he ought to have, and than would consist with a close attendance to his duty as a follower of Christ. He seemed to hanker after his relations and family concerns, and he could not part easily and suitably from them, but they stuck to him. It may be he had bidden them <hi type="italic">farewell</hi> once, but <hi type="italic">Loth to depart bids oft farewell,</hi> and therefore he must bid them <hi type="italic">farewell</hi> once more, for they are <hi type="italic">at home at his house.</hi> (3.) That he was willing to enter into a temptation from his purpose of following Christ. To go and bid them <hi type="italic">farewell</hi> that were <hi type="italic">at home at his house</hi> would be to expose himself to the strongest solicitations imaginable to alter his resolution; for they would all be against it, and would <hi type="italic">beg</hi> and <hi type="italic">pray</hi> that he would not <hi type="italic">leave them.</hi> Now it was presumption in him to thrust himself into such a temptation. Those that resolve to walk with their Maker, and follow their Redeemer, must resolve that they will not so much as parley with their tempter. <div eID="gen25715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25716" type="x-p"/> 2. The rebuke which Christ gave him for this request (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.62">v. 62</reference>): "<hi type="italic">No man, having put his hand to the plough,</hi> and designing to make good work of his ploughing, will <hi type="italic">look back,</hi> or look behind him, for then he makes balks with his plough, and the ground he ploughs is <hi type="italic">not fit</hi> to be sown; so thou, if thou hast a design to follow me and to reap the advantages of those that do so, yet if thou <hi type="italic">lookest back</hi> to a worldly life again and hankerest after that, if thou <hi type="italic">lookest back</hi> as Lot's wife did to Sodom, which seems to be alluded to here, <hi type="italic">thou art not fit for the kingdom of God.</hi>" (1.) "Thou art not <hi type="italic">soil</hi> fit to receive the <hi type="italic">good seed</hi> of the kingdom of God if thou art thus <hi type="italic">ploughed</hi> by the <hi type="italic">halves,</hi> and not gone through with." (2.) "Thou art not a <hi type="italic">sower</hi> fit to <hi type="italic">scatter</hi> the good seed of the kingdom if thou canst <hi type="italic">hold the plough</hi> no better." Ploughing is in order to sowing. As those are not fit to be <hi type="italic">sown</hi> with divine comforts whose <hi type="italic">fallow ground</hi> is not first <hi type="italic">broken up,</hi> so those are not fit to be employed in sowing who know not how to break up the fallow ground, but, when they have <hi type="italic">laid their hand to the plough,</hi> upon every occasion look back and think of quitting it. Note, Those who begin with the work of God must resolve to <hi type="italic">go on</hi> with it, or they will make nothing of it. Looking back inclines to <hi type="italic">drawing back,</hi> and <hi type="italic">drawing back</hi> is to <hi type="italic">perdition.</hi> Those are not fit for heaven who, having set their faces heavenward, face about. But he, and he only, that <hi type="italic">endures to the end, shall be saved.</hi>  <chapter eID="Luke.9"/> <div eID="gen25716" type="x-p"/>

Herod Troubled at What He Hears of Christ Desires to See Him.</title> <div sID="gen27898" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.14-Mark.6.30">Mr 6:14-30</reference>). <div eID="gen27898" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb031c2f37618c34db050823b5cb667c4dfcbbdd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14408"/><div sID="gen27899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14408"/><hi type="bold">7. perplexed--</hi>at a loss, embarrassed.<div eID="gen27899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">said of some, that John was risen--</hi>Among many opinions, this was the one which Herod himself adopted, for the reason, no doubt, mentioned on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.14">Mr 6:14</reference>. <div eID="gen27900" type="x-p"/>
entries.5754532aebb2dbf2d6f7ade99b030260e4eedca8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14409"/><div sID="gen27901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14409"/><hi type="bold">9. desired to see him--</hi>but did not, till as a prisoner He was sent to him by Pilate just before His death, as we learn from <reference osisRef="Luke.23.8">Lu 23:8</reference>.<div eID="gen27901" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.9.10-Luke.9.17">Lu 9:10-17</reference>. On the Return of the Twelve Jesus Retires with Them to Bethsaida, and There Miraculously Feeds Five Thousand.</title> <div sID="gen27902" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.31-Mark.6.44">Mr 6:31-44</reference>).<div eID="gen27902" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.9.18-Luke.9.27">Lu 9:18-27</reference>. Peter's Confession of Christ--Our Lord's First Explicit Announcement of His Approaching Death, and Warnings Arising Out of It.</title> <div sID="gen27903" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.16.13-Matt.16.28">Mt 16:13-28</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Mark.8.34">Mr 8:34</reference>). <div eID="gen27903" type="x-p"/>
entries.691a82cfe4283aa9d95c2c1ac1d69883fab63588: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14410"/><div sID="gen27904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14410"/><hi type="bold">24. will save--</hi>"Is minded to save," bent on saving. The pith of this maxim depends--as often in such weighty sayings (for example, "Let the dead bury the dead," <reference osisRef="Matt.8.22">Mt 8:22</reference>)--on the double sense attached to the word "life," a lower and a higher, the natural and the spiritual, temporal and eternal. An entire sacrifice of the lower, or a willingness to make it, is indispensable to the preservation of the higher life; and he who cannot bring himself to surrender the one for the sake of the other shall eventually lose both. <div eID="gen27904" type="x-p"/>
entries.8875412c01ab66fcce57922f711e037e517280ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14411"/><div sID="gen27905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14411"/><hi type="bold">26. ashamed of me, and of my words--</hi>The sense of shame is one of the strongest in our nature, one of the social affections founded on our love of reputation, which causes instinctive aversion to what is fitted to lower it, and was given us as a preservative from all that is properly shameful. When one is, in this sense of it, lost to shame, he is nearly past hope (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.5">Zec 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.15">Jr 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">3:3</reference>). But when Christ and "His words"--Christianity, especially in its more spiritual and uncompromising features--are unpopular, the same instinctive desire to stand well with others begets the temptation to be ashamed of Him, which only the 'expulsive power' of a higher affection can effectually counteract.<div eID="gen27905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh, &c.--</hi>He will render to that man his own treatment; He will disown him before the most august of all assemblies, and put him to "shame and everlasting contempt" (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Da 12:2</reference>). "Oh shame, to be put to shame before God, Christ, and angels!" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen27906" type="x-p"/>
entries.8693ee4d13d85afd219570ad0b8e85c6ec97f235: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14412"/><div sID="gen27907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14412"/><hi type="bold">27. not taste of death fill they see the kingdom of God--</hi>"see it come with power" (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.1">Mr 9:1</reference>); or see "the Son of man coming in His kingdom" (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.28">Mt 16:28</reference>). The reference, beyond doubt, is to the firm establishment and victorious progress, in the lifetime of some then present, of that new Kingdom of Christ, which was destined to work the greatest of all changes on this earth, and be the grand pledge of His final coming in glory. <div eID="gen27907" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5db2a762dd40814f5e47e134cfc131c79d8cf63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14413"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.9.28-Luke.9.36">Lu 9:28-36</reference>. Jesus Transfigured.</title> <div sID="gen27908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14413"/><hi type="bold">28. an eight days after these sayings--</hi>including the day on which this was spoken and that of the Transfiguration. Matthew and Mark say (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.1">Mt 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.9.2">Mr 9:2</reference>) "after six days," excluding these two days. As the "sayings" so definitely connected with the transfiguration scene are those announcing His death--at which Peter and all the Twelve were so startled and scandalized--so this scene was designed to show to the eyes as well as the heart how glorious that death was in the view of Heaven.<div eID="gen27908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Peter, James, and John--</hi>partners before in secular business; now sole witnesses of the resurrection of Jairus' daughter (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.37">Mr 5:37</reference>), the transfiguration, and the agony in the garden (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.33">Mr 14:33</reference>).<div eID="gen27909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a mountain--</hi>not Tabor, according to long tradition, with which the facts ill comport, but some one near the lake.<div eID="gen27910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to pray--</hi>for the period He had now reached was a critical and anxious one. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.16.13">Mt 16:13</reference>). But who can adequately translate those "strong cryings and tears?" Methinks, as I steal by His side, I hear from Him these plaintive sounds, "Lord, who hath believed Our report? I am come unto Mine own and Mine own receive Me not; I am become a stranger unto My brethren, an alien to My mother's children: Consider Mine enemies, for they are many, and they hate Me with cruel hatred. Arise, O Lord, let not man prevail. Thou that dwellest between the cherubim, shine forth: Show Me a token for good: Father, glorify Thy name." <div eID="gen27911" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0863137c1e9d30e0a147cba06a7757c448013a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14414"/><div sID="gen27912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14414"/><hi type="bold">29. as he prayed, the fashion, &c.--</hi>Before He cried He was answered, and while He was yet speaking He was heard. Blessed interruption to prayer this! Thanks to God, transfiguring manifestations are not quite strangers here. Ofttimes in the deepest depths, out of groanings which cannot be uttered, God's dear children are suddenly transported to a kind of heaven upon earth, and their soul is made as the chariots of Amminadab. Their prayers fetch down such light, strength, holy gladness, as make their face to shine, putting a kind of celestial radiance upon it (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Exod.34.29-Exod.34.35">Ex 34:29-35</reference>).<div eID="gen27912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raiment white, &c.--</hi>Matthew says, "His face did shine as the sun" (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.2">Mt 17:2</reference>), and Mark says (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.3">Mr 9:3</reference>), "His raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow, so as no fuller on earth can white them" (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.3">Mr 9:3</reference>). The light, then, it would seem, shone not upon Him from without, but out of Him from within; He was all irradiated, was in one blaze of celestial glory. What a contrast to that "visage more marred than men, and His form than the sons of men!" (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.14">Is 52:14</reference>). <div eID="gen27913" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d3774de15da2898ad476cc6d447931d402bf902: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14415"/><div sID="gen27914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14415"/><hi type="bold">30-31. there talked with him two men ... Moses and Elias ... appeared in glory--</hi>"Who would have believed these were not angels had not their human names been subjoined?" [Bengel]. (Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.1.10">Ac 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.16.5">Mr 16:5</reference>). Moses represented "the law," Elijah "the prophets," and both together the whole testimony of the Old Testament Scriptures, and the Old Testament saints, to Christ; now not borne in a book, but by living men, not to a coming, but a come Messiah, visibly, for they "appeared," and audibly, for they "spake." <div eID="gen27914" type="x-p"/>
entries.5704bb05b97df3fb65588bf36971d74b8f6b4464: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14417"/><div sID="gen27919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14417"/><hi type="bold">32. and when they were awake--</hi>so, certainly, the most commentators: but if we translate literally, it should be "but having kept awake" [Meyer, Alford]. Perhaps "having roused themselves up" [Olshausen] may come near enough to the literal sense; but from the word used we can gather no more than that they shook off their drowsiness. It was night, and the Lord seems to have spent the whole night on the mountain (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.37">Lu 9:37</reference>).<div eID="gen27919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saw his glory, &c.--</hi>The emphasis lies on "saw," qualifying them to become "eye-witnesses of His majesty" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.16">2Pe 1:16</reference>). <div eID="gen27920" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1d299ed336ba1d8ca3eaa0a98908795a216b963: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14418"/><div sID="gen27921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14418"/><hi type="bold">33. they departed--</hi>Ah! bright manifestations in this vale of tears are always "departing" manifestations. <div eID="gen27921" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3925da9f5f78c7219b9e7494defa3c835b38a41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14419"/><div sID="gen27922" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14419"/><hi type="bold">34-35. a cloud--</hi>not one of our watery clouds, but the Shekinah-cloud (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.23.39">Mt 23:39</reference>), the pavilion of the manifested presence of God with His people, what Peter calls "the excellent" of "magnificent glory" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.17">2Pe 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen27922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a voice--</hi>"such a voice," says Peter emphatically; "and this voice [he adds] we heard, when we were with Him in the holy mount" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.17">2Pe 1:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen27923" type="x-p"/>
entries.428b7870af8fd352de9b4113d73bbdba68ddef16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14421"/><div sID="gen27925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14421"/><hi type="bold">36. Jesus was found alone--</hi>Moses and Elias are gone. Their work is done, and they have disappeared from the scene, feeling no doubt with their fellow servant the Baptist, "He must increase, but I must decrease." The cloud too is gone, and the naked majestic Christ, braced in spirit, and enshrined in the reverent affection of His disciples, is left--to suffer!<div eID="gen27925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kept it close--</hi>feeling, for once at least, that such things were unmeet as yet for the general gaze.<div eID="gen27926" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.9.37-Luke.9.45">Lu 9:37-45</reference>. Demoniac and Lunatic Boy Healed--Christ's Second Explicit Announcement of his Death and Resurrection.</title> <div sID="gen27927" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.9.14-Mark.9.32">Mr 9:14-32</reference>.) <div eID="gen27927" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3667e589c5b463c74eaef8673375069bd61ad73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14422"/><div sID="gen27928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14422"/><hi type="bold">43-45. the mighty power of God--</hi>"the majesty" or "mightiness" of God in this last miracle, the transfiguration, &c.: the divine grandeur of Christ rising upon them daily. By comparing <reference osisRef="Matt.17.22">Mt 17:22</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Mark.9.30">Mr 9:30</reference>, we gather that this had been the subject of conversation between the Twelve and their Master as they journeyed along. <div eID="gen27928" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f9e63b783ba71b86d6ff236c60bd4d806d4a5db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14425"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.9.46-Luke.9.48">Lu 9:46-48</reference>. Strife among the Twelve Who Should Be Greatest--John Rebuked for Exclusiveness.</title> <div sID="gen27931" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14425"/>46-48. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.18.1-Matt.18.5">Mt 18:1-5</reference>). <div eID="gen27931" type="x-p"/>
entries.95daf7e1835441b3ef74a53bae866aa8580b6825: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14426"/><div sID="gen27932" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14426"/><hi type="bold">49-50. John answered, &c.--</hi>The link of connection here with the foregoing context lies in the words "in My name" (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.48">Lu 9:48</reference>). "Oh, as to that," said John, young, warm, but not sufficiently apprehending Christ's teaching in these things, "we saw one casting out devils in Thy name, and we forbade him: Were we wrong?" "Ye were wrong." "But we did because he followeth not us,'" "No matter. For (1) There is no man which shall do a miracle in My name that can lightly [soon] speak evil of Me' [Mr 9:39]. And (2) If such a person cannot be supposed to be 'against us,' you are to consider him 'for us.'" Two principles of immense importance. Christ does not say this man should not have followed "with them," but simply teaches how he was to be regarded though he did not--as a reverer of His name and a promoter of His cause. Surely this condemns not only those horrible attempts by force to shut up all within one visible pale of discipleship, which have deluged Christendom with blood in Christ's name, but the same spirit in its milder form of proud ecclesiastic scowl upon all who "after the form which they call a sect (as the word signifies, <reference osisRef="Acts.24.14">Ac 24:14</reference>), do so worship the God of their fathers." Visible unity in Christ's Church is devoutly to be sought, but this is not the way to it. See the noble spirit of Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.11.24-Num.11.29">Nu 11:24-29</reference>). <div eID="gen27932" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2237a1c3445c28037651dd503af653862cc97e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14427"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.9.51-Luke.9.56">Lu 9:51-56</reference>. The Period of His Assumption Approaching Christ Takes His Last Leave of Galilee--The Samaritans Refuse to Receive Him.</title> <div sID="gen27933" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14427"/><hi type="bold">51. the time was come--</hi>rather, "the days were being fulfilled," or approaching their fulfilment.<div eID="gen27933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27934" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he should be received up--</hi>"of His assumption," meaning His exaltation to the Father; a sublime expression, taking the sweep of His whole career, as if at one bound He was about to vault into glory. The work of Christ in the flesh is here divided into two great stages; all that preceded this belonging to the one, and all that follows it to the other. During the one, He formally "came to His own," and "would have gathered them"; during the other, the awful consequences of "His own receiving Him not" rapidly revealed themselves.<div eID="gen27934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he steadfastly set his face--</hi>the "He" here is emphatic--"He Himself then." See His own prophetic language, "I have set my face like a flint" (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Is 50:7</reference>).<div eID="gen27935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go to Jerusalem--</hi>as His goal, but including His preparatory visits to it at the feasts of tabernacles and of dedication (<reference osisRef="John.7.2">Joh 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.7.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.22">10:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.10.23">23</reference>), and all the intermediate movements and events. <div eID="gen27936" type="x-p"/>
entries.6bcaff8befa7ca844033d40df35995d76e1416ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14428"/><div sID="gen27937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14428"/><hi type="bold">52. messengers before his face ... to make ready for him--</hi>He had not done this before; but now, instead of avoiding, He seems to court publicity--all now hastening to maturity. <div eID="gen27937" type="x-p"/>
entries.a53b10bfac11bfd875fa220bb1f81413fbcef643: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14429"/><div sID="gen27938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14429"/><hi type="bold">53. did not receive him, because, &c.--</hi>The Galileans, in going to the festivals at Jerusalem, usually took the Samaritan route [Josephus, Antiquities, 20.6.1], and yet seem to have met with no such inhospitality. But if they were asked to prepare quarters for the Messiah, in the person of one whose "face was as though He would go to Jerusalem," their national prejudices would be raised at so marked a slight upon their claims. (See on <reference osisRef="John.4.20">Joh 4:20</reference>). <div eID="gen27938" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e55ae3dbc0ca95c9aaaa7b2fa14473df571ea16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14430"/><div sID="gen27939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14430"/><hi type="bold">54. James and John--</hi>not Peter, as we should have expected, but those "sons of thunder" (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.17">Mr 3:17</reference>), who afterwards wanted to have all the highest honors of the Kingdom to themselves, and the younger of whom had been rebuked already for his exclusiveness (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.49">Lu 9:49</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.50">50</reference>). Yet this was "the disciple whom Jesus loved," while the other willingly drank of His Lord's bitter cup. (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.10.38-Mark.10.40">Mr 10:38-40</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Acts.12.2">Ac 12:2</reference>). That same fiery zeal, in a mellowed and hallowed form, in the beloved disciple, we find in 2Jo 5:10; 3Jo 10.<div eID="gen27939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire ... as Elias--</hi>a plausible case, occurring also in Samaria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.10-2Kgs.1.12">2Ki 1:10-12</reference>). <div eID="gen27940" type="x-p"/>
entries.85c697f70e27bfbeb368b38711f9379f6f952425: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14431"/><div sID="gen27941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14431"/><hi type="bold">55-56. know not what ... spirit--</hi>The thing ye demand, though in keeping with the legal, is unsuited to the genius of the evangelical dispensation. The sparks of unholy indignation would seize readily enough on this example of Elias, though our Lord's rebuke (as is plain from <reference osisRef="Luke.9.56">Lu 9:56</reference>) is directed to the principle involved rather than the animal heat which doubtless prompted the reference. "It is a golden sentence of Tillotson, Let us never do anything for religion which is contrary to religion" [Webster and Wilkinson]. <div eID="gen27941" type="x-p"/>
entries.43002de90f4fcf0a27ef7b66552c830b5c67ac26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14433"/><div sID="gen27949" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14433"/><hi type="bold">61. I will follow ... but--</hi>The second disciple had a "but" too--a difficulty in the way just then. Yet the different treatment of the two cases shows how different was the spirit of the two, and to that our Lord addressed Himself. The case of Elisha (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.19-1Kgs.19.21">1Ki 19:19-21</reference>), though apparently similar to this, will be found quite different from the "looking back" of this case, the best illustration of which is that of those Hindu converts of our day who, when once persuaded to leave their spiritual fathers in order to "bid them farewell which are at home at their house," very rarely return to them. (Also see on <reference osisRef="Matt.8.21">Mt 8:21</reference>.) <div eID="gen27949" type="x-p"/>
entries.674885c52b2522579da5d9b0aec4b2175ef8809b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14434"/><div sID="gen27950" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14434"/><hi type="bold">62. No man, &c.--</hi>As ploughing requires an eye intent on the furrow to be made, and is marred the instant one turns about, so will they come short of salvation who prosecute the work of God with a distracted attention, a divided heart. Though the reference seems chiefly to ministers, the application is general. The expression "looking back" has a manifest reference to "Lot's wife" (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.26">Ge 19:26</reference>; and see on <reference osisRef="Luke.17.32">Lu 17:32</reference>). It is not actual return to the world, but a reluctance to break with it. (Also see on <reference osisRef="Matt.8.21">Mt 8:21</reference>.) <chapter eID="Luke.9"/>

entries.c73f620a47aee74d356d28b5b2d11b5a0d06920b: <div eID="gen40355" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen40356" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen40357" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen40357" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen40356" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen40358" type="x-p"/> Christ sends his apostles to preach and work miracles, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.1-Luk.9.6">Luk 9:1-6</reference>. Herod, hearing of the fame of Jesus, is perplexed; some suppose that John Baptist is risen from the dead; others, that Elijah or one of the old prophets was come to life, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.7-Luk.9.9">Luk 9:7-9</reference>. The apostles return and relate the success of their mission. He goes to a retired place, and the people follow him, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.10">Luk 9:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.11">Luk 9:11</reference>. He feeds five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.12-Luk.9.17">Luk 9:12-17</reference>. He asks his disciples what the public think of him, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.18-Luk.9.21">Luk 9:18-21</reference>. Foretells his passion, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.22">Luk 9:22</reference>. Shows the necessity of self-denial, and the importance of salvation, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.23-Luk.9.25">Luk 9:23-25</reference>. Threatens those who deny him before men, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.26">Luk 9:26</reference>. The transfiguration, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.27-Luk.9.36">Luk 9:27-36</reference>. Cures a demoniac, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.37-Luk.9.43">Luk 9:37-43</reference>. Again foretells his passion, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.44">Luk 9:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.45">Luk 9:45</reference>. The disciples contend who shall be greatest, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.46-Luk.9.48">Luk 9:46-48</reference>. Of the person who cast out devils in Christ's name, but did not associate with the disciples, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.49">Luk 9:49</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.50">Luk 9:50</reference>. Of the Samaritans who would not receive him, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.51-Luk.9.56">Luk 9:51-56</reference>. Of the man who wished to follow Jesus, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.57">Luk 9:57</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.58">Luk 9:58</reference>. He calls another disciple who asks permission first to bury his father, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.59">Luk 9:59</reference>. Our Lord's answer <reference osisRef="Luk.9.60-Luk.9.62">Luk 9:60-62</reference>. <div eID="gen40358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40359" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen40359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40360" type="x-p"/> Power and authority - Δυναμιν και εξουσιαν. The words properly mean here, the power to work miracles; and that authority by which the whole demoniac system was to be subjected to them. The reader will please to observe: <div eID="gen40360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40361" type="x-p"/> 1. That Luke mentions both demons and diseases; therefore he was either mistaken, or demons and diseases are not the same. <div eID="gen40361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40362" type="x-p"/> 2. The treatment of these two was not the same: - the demons were to be cast out, the diseases to be healed. See <reference osisRef="Mat.10.1">Mat 10:1</reference>.
entries.47fa068210eb4366527062b4e0bc36baeec8a358: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen40362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40363" type="x-p"/> To preach the kingdom of God - For an explication of this phrase, see on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.1">Mat 3:1</reference> (note).
entries.de8d3d454d7b9485858aa81afeef9fbe3f0df5f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen40363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40364" type="x-p"/> Take nothing - See on <reference osisRef="Mar.6.7">Mar 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.8">Mar 6:8</reference> (note). <div eID="gen40364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40365" type="x-p"/> Neither money - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.9">Mat 10:9</reference> (note). <div eID="gen40365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40366" type="x-p"/> Neither have two coats - Show that in all things ye are ambassadors for God; and go on his charges.
entries.108966409336f4cc71337b30637480c83cce8afb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen40366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40367" type="x-p"/> There abide, and thence depart - That is, remain in that lodging till ye depart from that city. Some MSS. and versions add μη, which makes the following sense: There remain, and depart Not thence. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.11">Mat 10:11</reference>.
entries.d481e4d9d640bb62cc49a633c86fdde543926fb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen40367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40368" type="x-p"/> Herod the tetrarch - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.2.1">Mat 2:1</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mat.14.1">Mat 14:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen40368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40369" type="x-p"/> By him - This is omitted by BCDL, two others, the Coptic, Sahidic, Armenian, and four of the Itala. It is probable that Luke might have written, Herod, hearing of all the things that were done, etc.; but Matthew says particularly, that it was the fame of Jesus of which he heard: <reference osisRef="Mat.14.1">Mat 14:1</reference>. <div eID="gen40369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40370" type="x-p"/> He was perplexed; - He was greatly perplexed διηπορει· from δια emphat. and απορεω, I am in perplexity. It is a metaphor taken from a traveler, who in his journey meets with several paths, one only of which leads to the place whither he would go; and, not knowing which to take, he is distressed with perplexity and doubt. The verb comes from α, negative, and πορος, a way or passage. A guilty conscience is a continual pest: - Herod had murdered John, and he is terribly afraid, lest he should arise from the dead, and bring his deeds to light, and expose him to that punishment which he deserved. See <reference osisRef="Mar.6.16">Mar 6:16</reference>.
entries.982e3e2017a1a044cca01006a2b58dd9796534da: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen40370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40371" type="x-p"/> Told him all - Related distinctly - διηγησαντο, from δια, through, and ἡγεομαι, I declare: hence the whole of this Gospel, because of its relating every thing so particularly, is termed διηγησις, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.1">Luk 1:1</reference>, a particular and circumstantially detailed narration. See on <reference osisRef="Mar.6.30">Mar 6:30</reference> (note).
entries.02acd589513ddeac27454fe3b4f802b816e8982e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen40371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40372" type="x-p"/> The people - followed him - Observe here five grand effects of Divine grace. <div eID="gen40372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40373" type="x-p"/> 1. The people are drawn to follow him. <div eID="gen40373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40374" type="x-p"/> 2. He kindly receives them. <div eID="gen40374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40375" type="x-p"/> 3. He instructs them in the things of God. <div eID="gen40375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40376" type="x-p"/> 4. He heals all their diseases. <div eID="gen40376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40377" type="x-p"/> 5. He feeds their bodies and their souls. See Quesnel. <div eID="gen40377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40378" type="x-p"/> Reader! Jesus is the same to the present moment. Follow him, and he will receive, instruct, heal, feed, and save thy soul unto eternal life.
entries.fa3ca338aa42b63dcd4bc87c09c0b8a5bdbb60ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen40378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40379" type="x-p"/> Send the multitude away - See this miracle explained at large, on the parallel places, <reference osisRef="Mat.14.15-Mat.14.21">Mat 14:15-21</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mar.6.36-Mar.6.44">Mar 6:36-44</reference> (note).
entries.dc9e6e8f1ee5d995bc2c4b6f96480876e0829aad: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen40379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40380" type="x-p"/> Then he took the five loaves - A minister of the Gospel, who is employed to feed souls, should imitate this conduct of Christ: <div eID="gen40380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40381" type="x-p"/> 1. He ought to exhort the people to hear with sedate and humble reverence. <div eID="gen40381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40382" type="x-p"/> 2. He should first take the bread of life himself, that he may be strengthened to feed others. <div eID="gen40382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40383" type="x-p"/> 3. He ought frequently to lift his soul to God, in order to draw down the Divine blessing on himself and his hearers. <div eID="gen40383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40384" type="x-p"/> 4. He should break the loaves - divide rightly the word of truth, and give to all such portions as are suited to their capacities and states. <div eID="gen40384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40385" type="x-p"/> 5. What he cannot perform himself, he should endeavor to effect by the ministry of others; employing every promising talent, for the edification of the whole, which he finds among the members of the Church of God. Under such a pastor, the flock of Christ will increase and multiply. See Quesnel.
entries.2b51cebfc05a692abcc399ab5be41610983b5dc0: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen40385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40386" type="x-p"/> Whom say the people - Οἱ οχλοι, the common people, i.e. the mass of the people. See this question considered on <reference osisRef="Mat.16.13">Mat 16:13</reference> (note), etc.
entries.5160e24e53194ce37ac66ef74857ece5b1c82b45: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen40386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40387" type="x-p"/> But whom say ye that I am? - Whom do ye tell the people that I am? What do ye preach concerning me? See also on <reference osisRef="Mat.16.14">Mat 16:14</reference> (note); and see the observations at the end of this chapter, (note). <div eID="gen40387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40388" type="x-p"/> The Christ of God - The Coptic and later Persic read, Thou art Christ God. After this comes in Peter's confession of our Lord, as related <reference osisRef="Mat.16.16">Mat 16:16</reference> (note), etc., where see the notes; and see also the observations of Granville Sharp, Esq., at the end of this chapter.
entries.956901d62842cb888e1782f096b04baab83415de: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen40388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40389" type="x-p"/> If any man will come after me - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.16.24">Mat 16:24</reference> (note), and on <reference osisRef="Mar.8.34">Mar 8:34</reference> (note), where the nature of proselytism among the Jews is explained. <div eID="gen40389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40390" type="x-p"/> Daily - Καθ' ἡμεραν is omitted by many reputable MSS., versions, and fathers. It is not found in the parallel places, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.24">Mat 16:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.8.34">Mar 8:34</reference>.
entries.55c8db2ce40e8c1aa435867f4bc7923e3e4f4938: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen40390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40391" type="x-p"/> Will save his life - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.16.24">Mat 16:24</reference> (note), etc.
entries.446dd8520a8d02ef933fde21195dc39abdf685cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen40391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40392" type="x-p"/> Lose himself - That is, his life or soul. See the parallel places, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.25">Mat 16:25</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mar.8.35">Mar 8:35</reference> (note), and especially the note on the former. <div eID="gen40392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40393" type="x-p"/> Or be cast away? - Or receive spiritual damage η ζημιωθεις. I have added the word spiritual here, which I conceive to be necessarily implied. Because, if a man received only temporal damage in some respect or other, yet gaining the whole world must amply compensate him. But if he should receive spiritual damage - hurt to his soul in the smallest degree, the possession of the universe could not indemnify him. Earthly goods may repair earthly losses, but they cannot repair any breach that may be made in the peace or holiness of the soul. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.16.26">Mat 16:26</reference> (note).

entries.db4cd5769aaf542e39d5480f008214f835f5aa3e: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen40394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40395" type="x-p"/> About an eight days after - See the whole of this important transaction explained at large on <reference osisRef="Mat.17.1-Mat.17.13">Mat 17:1-13</reference> (note).
entries.d168aa68252c6bf4fdc52b70add4d716b8a80967: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen40395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40396" type="x-p"/> His decease - Την εξοδον αυτον, That going out (or death) of his. That peculiar kind of death - its nature, circumstances, and necessity being considered. Instead of εξοδον, thirteen MSS. have δοξαν, glory. They spoke of that glory of his, which he was about to fill up (πληρουν) at Jerusalem. The Ethiopic unites both readings. The death of Jesus was his glory, because, by it, he gained the victory over sin, death, and hell, and purchased salvation and eternal glory for a lost world.
entries.80e7fb373e0029baa6a658295f47157d6681a321: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen40396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40397" type="x-p"/> It is good for us to be here - Some MSS. add παντοτε, It is good for us to be Always here.
entries.be31e9a10810a3bf6f480d30f903e59afe552c46: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen40397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40398" type="x-p"/> This is my beloved Son - Instead of ὁ αγαπητος, the beloved one, some MSS. and versions have εκλεκτος, the chosen one: and the Ethiopic translator, as in several other cases, to be sure of the true reading, retains both. <div eID="gen40398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40399" type="x-p"/> In whom I am well pleased, or have delighted - is added by some very ancient MSS. entries.6bf1173af33690ac3919648c1f0519d9e8c6f791: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen40399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40400" type="x-p"/> Much people - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.17.14">Mat 17:14</reference> (note).
entries.29735779904f27a3908993cfbcdd6b7dde21f441: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen40400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40401" type="x-p"/> A spirit taketh him, and he suddenly crieth out - Πνευμα λαμβανει αυτον. This very phrase is used by heathen writers, when they speak of supernatural influence. The following, from Herodotus, will make the matter, I hope, quite plain. Speaking of Scyles, king of the Scythians, who was more fond of Grecian manners and customs than of those of his countrymen, and who desired to be privately initiated into the Bacchic mysteries, he adds: "Now because the Scythians reproach the Greeks with these Bacchanals, and say that to imagine a god driving men into paroxysms of madness is not agreeable to sound reason, a certain Borysthenian, while the king was performing the ceremonies of initiation, went out, and discovered the matter to the Scythian army in these words: 'Ye Scythians ridicule us because we celebrate the Bacchanals, και ἡμεας ὁ θεος ΛΑΜΒΑΝΕΙ, and the God Possesses Us: but now the same demon, οὑτος ὁ δαιμων, has Taken Possession, ΛΕΛΑΒΗΚΕ, of your king, for he celebrates the Bacchanals, and ὑπο του θεου μαινεται, is filled with fury by this god." Herodot. l. iv. p. 250, edit. Gale. <div eID="gen40401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40402" type="x-p"/> This passage is exceedingly remarkable. The very expressions which Luke uses here are made use of by Herodotus. A demon, δαιμων, is the agent in the Greek historian, and a demon is the agent in the case mentioned in the text, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.42">Luk 9:42</reference>. In both cases it is said the demon possesses the persons, and the very same word, λαμβανει is used to express this in both historians. Both historians show that the possessions were real, by the effects produced in the persons: the heathen king rages with fury through the influence of the demon called the god Bacchus; the person in the text screams out, (κραζει), is greatly convulsed, and foams at the mouth. Here was a real possession, and such as often took place among those who were worshippers of demons.
entries.9104755e812deb7668166dc2f60325c2b69e59a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen40402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40403" type="x-p"/> The devil threw him down, and tare him - See this case considered at large, on <reference osisRef="Mat.17.15-Mat.17.18">Mat 17:15-18</reference> (note), and on <reference osisRef="Mar.9.14-Mar.9.27">Mar 9:14-27</reference> (note).
entries.950cbc5c4a321622bdeb349e2cfc59aebdbf9d0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen40403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40404" type="x-p"/> The mighty power - This majesty of God, μεγαλειοτητι του Θεου. They plainly saw that it was a case in which any power inferior to that of God could be of no avail; and they were deeply struck with the majesty of God manifested in the conduct of the blessed Jesus.
entries.92602dac8370847dd0beb16164d590a1ca8fc05e: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen40404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40405" type="x-p"/> Let these sayings sink down into your ears - Or, put these words into your ears. To other words, you may lend occasional attention, but to what concerns my sufferings and death you must ever listen. Let them constantly occupy a place in your most serious meditations and reflections.

entries.2936f21ed2f83a9e50eaac5e162f93c900e2b85f: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen40406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40407" type="x-p"/> There arose a reasoning - Εισηλθε δε διαλογισμος, A dialogue took place - one inquired, and another answered, and so on.
